articles.title: Frailty and Hospitalization After Emergency Department Evaluation Within Triage Categories in Older Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal_full: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Triage reflects acute urgency, whereas frailty may also influence disposition in older emergency department (ED) patients. This study aimed to estimate the association between Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)-defined frailty and hospitalization after ED evaluation within Japan Triage and Acuity Scale (JTAS) categories and assess whether the strength varied across triage categories.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study in an urban tertiary hospital in Japan. We identified consecutive triaged ED visits by patients aged ≥ 65 years from November 2025 to March 2026. Visits with CFS scores and covariates constituted the complete-case cohort. CFS ≥ 5 was defined as frailty. The primary outcome was admission to the study hospital or acute-care interhospital transfer. We used a mixed-effects logistic regression model with a CFS-by-JTAS interaction term, adjusting for age, sex, mode of arrival, injury- or poisoning-related visit, living arrangement, and long-term care needs certification, with patient-level random intercept. The global interaction was assessed using a likelihood-ratio test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 3127 ED visits, 1526 resulted in hospitalization. In JTAS 1, the adjusted odds ratio (OR) for CFS ≥ 5 was not estimated because of quasi-complete separation. In the model excluding JTAS 1, the adjusted OR was 1.00 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65-1.55) in JTAS 2, 1.54 (95% CI: 1.19-1.99) in JTAS 3, and 2.01 (95% CI: 1.13-3.58) in JTAS 4/5. The global CFS-by-JTAS interaction was not statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.091).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Category-specific estimates suggested little association in JTAS 2 but were numerically larger in JTAS 3 and JTAS 4/5. However, the global interaction was nonsignificant, providing insufficient evidence that the association differed across categories. Prospective studies should examine the clinical, geriatric, social, decision-related, and healthcare-system factors that may underlie this association among older patients with comparable triage-assessed urgency.

articles.title: Epidemiology and Quality of Care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples Treated by Emergency Medical Services for Stroke in Victoria, Australia: Retrospective Analysis of Linked Data.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To examine the epidemiology of stroke and transient ischaemic attack (TIA), and quality of care provided to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ('Indigenous') patients presenting to emergency medical services (EMSs) with stroke or TIA.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective population-based data linkage study.

abstract.label: SETTING, PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Victoria, Australia. Patients aged ≥ 18 years with hospital-confirmed stroke or TIA who presented to EMSs between 1 January 2015 and 30 June 2019 and were successfully linked with hospital or mortality datasets.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
abstract.text: Thirty- and 90-day mortality, crude and age-standardised incidence rates, EMS quality of care.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 32,163 patients, 287 (0.9%) were Indigenous. Indigenous patients were younger than non-Indigenous patients (median age, 62 vs. 77 years, p < 0.001). Age-standardised incidence of EMS attendance was higher within the Indigenous population (343 vs. 144 per 100,000 person-years; incidence rate ratio, 2.383 [95% confidence interval (CI), 2.084-2.711]). Rates of call-taker identification of stroke or TIA and hospital diagnoses were comparable; however, Indigenous patients were less likely to receive a stroke assessment from paramedics (166/285 [58.2%] vs. 21,271/31,605 [67.3%]; p = 0.001) and more frequently taken to stroke-capable hospitals (257/275 [93.5%] vs. 27,371/30,647 [89.3%]; p = 0.027), but less frequently taken to endovascular thrombectomy-capable hospitals (67/275 [24.4%] vs. 10,015/30,647 [32.7%]; p = 0.003). Adjusted mortality was similar between groups (30 days: hazard ratio, 0.814 [95% CI, 0.518-1.279]; 90 days: hazard ratio, 0.805 [95% CI, 0.534-1.214]). However, age-standardised incidence of 90-day mortality was higher within the Indigenous population (39 vs. 24 per 100,000 person-years; incidence rate ratio, 1.621 [95% CI, 1.031-2.398]). Indigenous patients also more often recontacted EMSs for any reason within 90 days (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.548 [95% CI, 1.194-2.007]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The age-standardised incidence of EMS attendance for stroke in the Indigenous population was more than double that for the non-Indigenous population. Although there was no difference in stroke identification at the time of the emergency call, Indigenous patients were less likely to be evaluated by paramedics for stroke.

articles.title: Reducing Peripheral Intravenous Catheter Use in Adult Acute Care: A Systematic Review.

abstract.text: Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are the most frequently inserted invasive device in acute care, yet up to 52% remain unused, exposing patients to avoidable risks and increasing healthcare costs. Despite growing awareness of inappropriate PIVC use, unnecessary insertion persists, driven by cultural and organisational norms and risk-averse practices. Interventions to reduce PIVC use have been implemented, but their effectiveness and sustainability have not been systematically synthesised. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251033201). Searches of CINAHL, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science identified studies reporting interventions to reduce PIVC insertion, unused PIVCs, and common complications. Data were extracted for intervention characteristics and PIVC outcomes. Implementation strategies were mapped to Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research domains for summative analysis. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed when appropriate. Twelve studies were included from emergency departments and inpatient settings across high-income countries. Most reported reductions in PIVC insertion and unused catheters, with improvements in secondary outcomes including phlebitis and bloodstream infections. Sustainability of practice change was demonstrated in two multi-year follow-up studies. Interventions showed a significant trend for increasing complexity over time, with recent strategies incorporating multi-modal, theory-informed approaches. Meta-analysis showed substantial heterogeneity, limiting pooled estimate interpretation, while methodological limitations restricted causal inference. Multi-modal interventions addressing behavioural, organisational, and contextual determinants appear most effective for reducing PIVC insertion rates and unnecessary PIVC use. Future research should evaluate sustainability, cost-effectiveness, and scalability using implementation science frameworks.

articles.title: Co-Design of a Theory-Informed, Multicomponent, Intervention for Diagnostic Stewardship in a Major-Referral Emergency Department: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Low-value diagnostic tests harm patients. Stewardship of tests can improve patient safety. Co-design and behavioural change theories can enhance the effectiveness of diagnostic stewardship interventions. This study aimed to co-design a theory-informed diagnostic stewardship intervention at a major-referral emergency department in Queensland, Australia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A qualitative study was conducted at Townsville University Hospital Emergency Department. The Theoretical Domains Framework underpinned intervention design. Emergency clinicians ordering pathology tests were eligible for inclusion. A purposive sample of consenting participants was recruited. Data were collected via workshops facilitated by the lead author. Conversations were audio recorded and digitally transcribed. Data were managed with NVivo. Data were analysed by inductive and deductive approaches to generate codes, categories and themes. Thematic saturation and optimal stakeholder engagement influenced the final sample size. Trustworthiness was ensured via reflexivity, audit trail, thick description and participant validation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seven workshops were conducted with 35 emergency physicians (18 male, 17 female) with a range of specialist experience (1-31 years). Urine culture was the diagnostic test of choice. Culture, complexity, and efficiency were identified as the major drivers of low-value urine cultures. Education, nudge, clinical champions, and audit/feedback were selected as intervention components. Credibility of change and workflow inefficiency were perceived as intervention challenges.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Stakeholder engagement has enhanced perceived acceptability of this co-designed intervention for urine culture diagnostic stewardship. Behavioural change theories strengthen co-designed interventions by addressing context-specific drivers of low-value tests. Co-design and behavioural change theories can inform bespoke interventions to nurture a culture of diagnostic stewardship in emergency medicine practice.

articles.title: Prospective Study of Ultrasound-Guided Regional Anesthesia Blocks for Upper Extremity Procedures in a Community Emergency Medicine Hospital.

abstract.text: Painful upper extremity injuries frequently require procedures for which procedural sedation may be resource-intensive. This prospective study evaluated the educational impact and clinical feasibility of implementing a structured ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia curriculum as an alternative to procedural sedation for selected upper extremity procedures within a community emergency medicine residency. From January through December 2025, attending emergency physicians participated in a two-hour didactic session and hands-on workshop followed by longitudinal on-shift mentorship. Physician knowledge was assessed using a locally developed pre- and post-intervention cognitive assessment. Seventeen physicians completed the curriculum. Mean assessment scores increased from 8.18±3.05 to 18.41±1.58, with a mean improvement of 10.24 points (95% confidence interval (CI), 9.02-11.45; p<0.001). During clinical implementation, 30 ultrasound-guided brachial plexus blocks were performed. The intended procedure was completed without procedural sedation in 28 (93.3%) cases. In two (6.7%) cases, procedural sedation was subsequently required to complete the planned reduction. No immediate procedure-related complications were observed. A structured ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia curriculum was associated with improved physician knowledge and successful clinical implementation of brachial plexus blocks. These findings support the feasibility of incorporating ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia as an additional analgesic strategy for selected upper extremity procedures in a community emergency medicine setting.

articles.title: Mechanism-specific structural patterns in hospitalized severe mechanical open-globe injury: Implications for triage and operative preparedness in a 13-year tertiary referral cohort.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Severe mechanical open-globe injury (OGI) is a vision-threatening emergency. Injury mechanism is often available at first contact, whereas definitive structural classification may emerge only after clinical and operative assessment. We examined whether hospitalized severe mechanical OGI shows mechanism-specific structural patterns and whether final structural phenotype is associated with short-term inpatient course.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort of 1096 index hospitalizations for severe mechanical OGI during 2013-2025 at a tertiary referral center in eastern China. Injury mechanisms were adjudicated from free-text cause fields using a prespecified coding framework. The primary outcome was final Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology (BETT) phenotype. Mechanism-phenotype associations were assessed using an L2-penalized multinomial logistic model adjusted for age, sex, and calendar year; exponentiated contrasts were reported as adjusted odds ratios. Secondary classification-to-course analyses evaluated early visual status, visual-category improvement, length of stay, procedural burden, and treatment non-completion, with presenting visual acuity added to secondary models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Industrial metal injury was the dominant mechanism (45.5%), followed by plastic/other foreign-body injury (9.7%) and falls (7.2%). Mechanism was strongly associated with final BETT phenotype (Pearson χ² = 425.62, p < 0.001). Industrial metal injury clustered toward intraocular foreign body (IOFB)-related injury and laceration without IOFB (37.3% and 36.3%), whereas falls and fireworks were rupture-dominant (96.2% and 96.0%). In the adjusted multinomial model, falls were strongly associated with globe rupture rather than laceration without IOFB compared with industrial metal injury (adjusted OR 27.40, 95% CI 12.71-77.54). Globe rupture showed the most severe inpatient course: 79.6% presented with light perception/no light perception, 94.0% had poor discharge visual acuity, and 34.3% had documented treatment non-completion. After additional adjustment for presenting visual acuity, rupture remained associated with poor discharge visual acuity (adjusted OR 5.25, 95% CI 2.84-9.71) and treatment non-completion (adjusted OR 3.78, 95% CI 2.19-6.52).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Hospitalized severe mechanical OGI exhibited mechanism-specific structural patterns that extended beyond anatomical classification by mapping onto short-term inpatient course. Mechanism may support early structural suspicion, operative preparedness, expectation management, and treatment-pathway counseling, complementing rather than replacing examination, imaging, and operative assessment.

articles.title: Caregiver Satisfaction and Experience With a Novel Device to Safely Transport Life-Sustaining Durable Medical Equipment.
articles.journal_full: Dimensions of critical care nursing : DCCN

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The novel Medical Equipment Adaptable Travel Restraint (MEATR) was created by 2 critical care nurses who recognized that individuals with life-sustaining durable medical equipment (DME) did not have a safe way to travel with their DME when leaving the hospital.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study aimed to understand the satisfaction and experience of participants utilizing the MEATR to transport their DME in a noncommercial motor vehicle.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This descriptive cohort study was conducted between June 2023 and March 2025 at 2 quaternary pediatric hospitals in the United States. To measure the satisfaction and experience of traveling with their child's DME, caregivers completed surveys before receiving the MEATR, then at 2 weeks and 2 months.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: One-hundred caregivers and their children participated. Most caregivers were 31 to 50 years of age (67.0%), female (91.0%), White (80.0%), and not Hispanic or Latino (80.0%). Most children were under 4 years of age (54.5%), male (54.5%), White (80.8%), and not Hispanic or Latino (74.7%). Before receiving the MEATR, 15.0% of caregivers reported they were satisfied with the way they transported their medical equipment. After using the MEATR, there was a significant increase in satisfaction with DME transport (92.1% and 94.1%; P<.001). Regarding experience, at the time of enrollment, most participants reported limiting their travel to certain places due to medical equipment (71.0%). This number decreased significantly after receiving the MEATR (16.9% and 17.8%; P<.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Participants who utilized the MEATR to transport their DME reported improved satisfaction and experience. Thus, the MEATR could improve the quality of life for individuals who require life-sustaining DME.

articles.title: Pediatric Emergency Care Variation: Might Normothetic Data Undermine Adaptive Expertise?

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Practice variation across physicians is commonly attributed to idiosyncratic tendencies. What factors contribute to physicians' practice variation in the disposition of children with asthma exacerbation? How do metrics demonstrating variation impact physicians and learners?

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this social constructivist qualitative study, we interviewed 11 Pediatric Emergency Medicine attendings, purposively sampling across a spectrum of acute asthma exacerbation admission rates. Participants reflected on their recent care of patients with asthma, how they assess patients, and how they determine disposition. They were shown a de-identified funnel plot demonstrating disposition rates across the physician group and reflected on the 1) quality of the metric and 2) impact on practice. We used reflexive thematic analysis to describe patterns across the data that addressed the study's research questions.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants cited factors at the patient, caregiver, clinical care team, clinical environment, and personal practice levels that might result in variation. Participants framed the ability to weigh these sometimes competing factors as a reflection of patient-centered care. But when presented with a group-level data display, participants were surprised by the variation, valued seeing how they practiced compared to peers, and sometimes expressed a willingness to alter their practices to be "nearer the mean."

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Some variation in care may be driven by physician adaptive expertise, which is not fully captured through metric-driven nomothetic data. Though metrics are fundamental to understanding practice patterns, decontextualized aggregations of data may risk minimizing, or even framing as deviant, the expertise exercised by physicians when they weigh multiple factors in decision-making.

articles.title: Non-Stop: A Decade of Integrating Health Systems Science Into Emergency Medicine Residency.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Despite the growing importance of Health Systems Science (HSS), many emergency medicine (EM) residency programs lack a formal, comprehensive curriculum for health policy and advocacy.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We developed a longitudinal Health Policy and Advocacy curriculum by mapping core components, based off those originally proposed in the New England Journal of Medicine, to ACGME milestones. The components were refined through expert ranking by physicians attending the ACEP Teaching Fellowship to identify high-yield topics specific to emergency medicine, such as the health care safety net, medical malpractice, and physician reimbursement.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The resulting curriculum encompasses six key domains: adverse events, medical errors and malpractice; health care safety net; quality indicators, measures, and outcomes; physician reimbursement; U.S. health care system, financing, and delivery; and the business of emergency medicine. Curricular implementation utilizes several different teaching models, incorporating asynchronous modules, didactic sessions, a coding and billing workshop, and a four-hour mock trial.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Integrating a structured health policy curriculum into EM training provides residents with essential non-clinical skills that are increasingly necessary to effective practice in today's health care environment. This innovation addresses a critical educational gap, preparing residents to become vocal advocates for their patients and the profession.

articles.title: Fixation-specific modeling of age-frailty interactions to predict early mortality after hip fracture surgery.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early mortality after hip fracture surgery remains high. Existing risk models treat age and frailty as independent predictors and may not reflect how physiologic reserve modifies risk across fixation strategies. We evaluated whether modeling age-frailty interactions improves estimation of 30-day mortality.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective cohort study using the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) database (2019-2023) included adults undergoing intramedullary nailing (IMN), hemiarthroplasty, or plate fixation for femoral neck, pertrochanteric, or subtrochanteric fractures. Frailty was measured using a validated 5-item modified frailty index. Generalized additive models with bivariate spline surfaces generated procedure-specific mortality risk estimates. Secondary outcomes were assessed using propensity score-matched cohorts.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 115,643 patients, 30-day mortality was 5.25%. Predicted mortality varied across age-frailty combinations, ranging from 1.41% to 28.83% for IMN, 1.26%-32.06% for hemiarthroplasty, and 0.48%-20.37% for plate fixation. IMN showed higher transfusion rates, while hemiarthroplasty demonstrated higher cardiopulmonary complication rates. Length of stay did not differ between procedures.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Modeling age and frailty as interacting variables produces procedure-specific mortality risk estimates after hip fracture surgery. These estimates support patient counseling and perioperative decision-making using routinely available clinical data.

articles.title: Hemodynamic Compromise Due to Semaglutide-Associated Abdominal Distension.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonists are becoming widely used, but commonly cause gastrointestinal side effects that are often mild but can occasionally be significant.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 35-year-old male patient with obesity and otherwise minimal medical history presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode that occurred several days after restarting high-dose GLP-1 agonist therapy. Imaging showed massive gastric distension with significant inferior vena cava compression. He developed low-output shock requiring very high-dose vasoactive medications, which resolved after gastric decompression via emesis, nasogastric tube placement, and intravenous fluid resuscitation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case represents a heretofore unseen side effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist administration, with initiation of maximum-dose semaglutide leading to dramatic gastric distension causing inferior vena cava compression and low-output shock.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: In patients with unexplained hypotension, shock, and/or syncope on glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist therapy, adverse medication effects should be considered as possible etiologies. This case emphasizes the importance of gradual dose escalation of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists under provider guidance.

articles.title: Is there Supporting Evidence for Routine Nil per Os Status in the Emergency Department? A Scoping Review.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The routine practice of keeping emergency department patients nil per os is widespread, often stemming from traditional inpatient protocols rather than emergency department--specific evidence. Although guidelines exist for nil per os before procedural sedation and analgesia, their universal application in the dynamic emergency department environment can lead to prolonged fasting, patient discomfort, and potential adverse outcomes, directly impacting nursing care and patient satisfaction. This scoping review aimed to summarize existing data on the efficacy and impact of nil per os status in emergency department patients and to evaluate the evidence supporting the traditional, routine nil per os practice during emergency department stays.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic scoping review was conducted using Medline, Embase, Web of Science, and CINAHL databases (inception to June 2025). Original studies assessing emergency department nil per os status on patient outcomes, including aspiration risk, vomiting, delays in emergent or urgent surgical procedures, and patient or provider satisfaction, were included.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Out of 2274 screened studies, 21 met the inclusion criteria. The majority (n = 13, 62%) evaluated fasting status and adverse outcomes following procedural sedation and analgesia in the emergency department. All 13 studies consistently found no significant association between patient fasting status and adverse events in adult and pediatric patients undergoing emergency department procedural sedation and analgesia. Furthermore, 6 studies analyzing nil per os duration for procedural sedation and analgesia also reported no statistically significant association with adverse events. Four studies revealed that most patients undergoing procedural sedation and analgesia in the emergency department did not adhere to established American Academy of Pediatrics/American Society of Anesthesiology fasting guidelines.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Despite its prevalence, this review identifies limited emergency department-specific evidence to support routine nil per os status, particularly beyond procedural sedation and analgesia. Most included studies focused on pediatric procedural sedation and analgesia populations, and the findings should therefore be interpreted cautiously when applied to adult and older adult populations. Among patients undergoing emergency department procedural sedation and analgesia, no association was found between preprocedural fasting and adverse events. Existing fasting guidelines are largely extrapolated from elective surgical populations rather than the emergency department setting. These findings support the re-evaluation of routine nil per os practices and reinforce the role of emergency nurses in advocating for individualized, evidence-based patient care.

articles.title: Small Grants, Big Impact: Outcomes of an Internal Excellence in Education Grant Program.

abstract.text: Evidence-based innovation is essential for advancing veterinary medical education, yet dedicated funding for educational research remains limited. In 2016, the Iowa State University College of Veterinary Medicine established the Excellence in Education Grant (EEG) program to provide competitive intramural funding for faculty-led educational research. This Best Practice report evaluates the first 8 years of the program and compares its outcomes with similar initiatives in human medical education. Administrative records, financial data, and project reports from seven funding cycles (2016-2024) were retrospectively reviewed. Outcomes evaluated included project completion, achievement of objectives, curricular implementation, creation of durable educational resources, scholarly dissemination, fiscal utilization, and investigator perceptions of the program. Twenty-three projects received a total of $287,836 in funding (mean award: $12,416); 21 projects proceeded to implementation. Of these, 81% achieved their stated objectives and 71% resulted in sustained curricular adoption, including integration of point-of-care ultrasound, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, antimicrobial stewardship, and faculty development initiatives. Nearly half of funded projects generated durable educational resources including simulation models and digital learning tools. Thirty-eight percent of projects produced conference presentations or peer-reviewed publications. Faculty consistently described the program as an important catalyst for educational innovation, scholarship, and professional development, particularly for clinician-educators. Although project timelines frequently required extension, these challenges informed subsequent improvements in program oversight and fiscal management. The EEG program demonstrates that relatively small institutional seed grants can generate substantial returns through sustained curricular innovation, educational scholarship, and faculty development, providing a practical and replicable best practice model for advancing veterinary medical education.

articles.title: Electrical Alternans as an Early Clue to a Rapidly Evolving Large Pericardial Effusion: The Role of Point-of-Care Ultrasound.

abstract.text: Electrical alternans is an uncommon electrocardiographic finding classically associated with significant pericardial effusion and may raise suspicion for cardiac tamponade in the appropriate clinical context. We report the case of a 65-year-old man who presented with 3 days of progressive dyspnea 10 days after hospitalization for acute pericarditis, during which transthoracic echocardiography showed no pericardial effusion. On presentation, he was tachycardic at 110 beats/min and had jugular venous distension, while electrocardiography demonstrated prominent electrical alternans. Although he was not hypotensive and had no overt evidence of hemodynamic compromise, the combination of recent pericarditis, progressive dyspnea, venous congestion, and electrical alternans raised immediate concern for a rapidly evolving large pericardial effusion with clinical features suggestive of cardiac tamponade. Point-of-care ultrasound rapidly demonstrated a large pericardial effusion, prompting urgent transfer for definitive evaluation and management. Within minutes of transfer, the patient's respiratory distress worsened despite persistently preserved vital signs, and urgent pericardial drainage was performed. Approximately 1,200 mL of grossly hemorrhagic pericardial fluid was evacuated, resulting in rapid and marked clinical improvement. This case highlights electrical alternans as an important early clinical clue to significant pericardial effusion and emphasizes the value of immediate point-of-care ultrasound in the emergency department when cardiac tamponade is clinically suspected. It also demonstrates the dynamic nature of pericardial disease, showing that a large pericardial effusion with clinical features suggestive of cardiac tamponade may develop within a short interval after a previously negative echocardiographic examination. Integrating electrocardiographic findings with rapid bedside ultrasound assessment may facilitate earlier recognition of evolving clinically significant pericardial disease and timely definitive intervention.

articles.title: Group ingestion of high-powered magnets in children-A clinical and public health challenge.

abstract.text: High-powered magnets are a preventable cause of serious gastrointestinal injury in children, with ingestion often resulting in hospitalization and occasionally surgery. We report six classmates, aged 5-6 years, who ingested high-powered magnets during a single school day after mistaking them for candy. All presented to our emergency department within 12 h of ingestion. Three underwent endoscopy and three were managed with serial imaging; all magnets were retrieved or passed spontaneously, with no obstruction, perforation, or surgery. The near-simultaneous presentations strained endoscopy resources and required coordinated triage by magnet number, configuration, and symptoms. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission defines these magnets for users ≥14 years, yet all patients were under 7, underscoring age-based labeling limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first reported cluster of simultaneous classroom magnet ingestion, highlighting persistent exposure despite regulation and the need for standardized triage protocols and national surveillance.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis of pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures: a deep learning-based clinical decision support model.
articles.journal_full: Journal of pediatric orthopedics. Part B

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Accurate detection of pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures remains a diagnostic challenge in emergency settings. To address this, we developed and validated a transfer-learning model, benchmarking its performance against board-certified emergency physicians. A retrospective dataset of 1440 anonymized pediatric elbow radiographs (720 fractures and 720 normal) was preprocessed using grayscale normalization, aspect-ratio-preserving resizing, adaptive denoising, and contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization. Data were split at the patient level into training and validation (n = 1295) and a held-out test set (n = 145). A pretrained ResNet50 backbone was fine-tuned, and model stability was assessed via five-fold stratified cross-validation. Clinical applicability was evaluated in a blinded reader study where 20 emergency physicians interpreted 200 radiographs. On the held-out test set, the model achieved 90.34% accuracy, 93.5% sensitivity, and 86.8% specificity. Five-fold cross-validation yielded a mean accuracy of 91.72%, sensitivity of 92.8%, and specificity of 88.5%. In the reader study, emergency physicians achieved a mean accuracy of 87.6%, sensitivity of 90.5%, and specificity of 84.7%. Diagnostic performance differences between the model and physicians were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). The transfer-learning model achieved clinician-comparable performance, indicating its potential utility as an initial triage tool. However, the algorithm shares human diagnostic limitations, exhibiting lower sensitivity for nondisplaced Gartland type I fractures. Therefore, based on current data, it cannot be concluded that artificial intelligence implementation will eliminate the risk of missed fractures. Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical deployment.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III (retrospective diagnostic study).

articles.title: Hospital-Level Acute Care at Home via Direct Home Admission in Taiwan: A Non-randomized Controlled Pilot Trial Before National Implementation.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hospital-at-home (HaH) models are emerging globally, but evidence for community-initiated HaH within Taiwan's Integrated Home-Based Medical Care system remains limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the clinical outcomes, patient/caregiver experience, and feasibility of a HaH model centered on direct home admission (DHA), with a small proportion entering through an emergency department-passed pathway.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Prospective non-randomized controlled pilot trial conducted between October 2022 and July 2023.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: A total of 144 homebound older adults (83 HaH; 61 brick-and-mortar hospital) with acute infections requiring hospital-level treatment across 5 hospitals and 13 community clinics. Participants were generally frail, chronically ill, and functionally dependent.

abstract.label: INTERVENTIONS
abstract.text: The HaH group received interprofessional visits, intravenous pharmacotherapy, point-of-care diagnostics, and remote patient monitoring. The control group received standard inpatient care.

abstract.label: MAIN MEASURES
abstract.text: Primary outcomes included remission/complete treatment, clinical escalation requiring hospital transfer, death during the treatment episode, and 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included length of stay (LOS), quality of life, and patient/caregiver satisfaction.

abstract.label: KEY RESULTS
abstract.text: Remission/complete treatment was achieved in most patients in both groups (86.7% vs. 95.1%; p = 0.153). Mortality during the treatment episode was low (2.4% vs. 3.3%; p = 1.000). Nine HaH patients (10.8%) required clinical escalation. The HaH group had a significantly shorter LOS (9.72 vs. 11.85 days; p = 0.035) and reported significantly higher satisfaction, convenience, and willingness to choose the model again (p < 0.05).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This pilot trial, the first to evaluate a DHA-based HaH model in Taiwan, provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and acceptability of community-initiated hospital-level acute care at home (ACAH) for frail older adults. These findings support the integration of hospital-level acute care into Taiwan's existing home-care infrastructure and informed the subsequent development of the national ACAH program.

articles.title: Development of consensus guidelines for classification of emergent neonatal transports using a Delphi process.
articles.journal_full: Journal of perinatology : official journal of the California Perinatal Association
authors: Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium (CHNC) Transport Focus Group

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The transport of neonates to tertiary and quaternary neonatal intensive care units occurs frequently in North America, particularly for neonates requiring emergent intervention. The timely stabilization and transfer of a critically ill neonate requiring higher level of care is imperative for optimal clinical outcomes. There is no consensus on the definition of "emergent" related to dispatch of a transport team. However, some utilize a time frame of 30 minutes from referral center request based on illness severity and/or risk. Current definitions of illness severity and/or risk are institution-specific, lacking standardization. The development of consensus-driven guidelines for emergent neonatal transport criteria will provide a framework adaptable across diverse healthcare settings to standardize decision making, resulting in comparable data and outcome measures.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The aim of this project is to develop expert consensus criteria for neonatal emergent interfacility transport.

abstract.label: DESIGN/METHODS
abstract.text: Following review of available literature and institution-specific guidelines and policies, a subset of neonatologists within the Children's Hospitals Neonatal Consortium (CHNC) Transport Focus Group compiled a proposed list of emergent neonatal criteria. These criteria were divided into three categories: (1) diagnosis, (2) clinical sign, or (3) specialized equipment and/or resources required. Using the Delphi process, CHNC transport leaders voted in two rounds for consensus.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Round 1 of surveys received responses from 31 of 49 (63%) CHNC sites and achieved 100% agreement on criteria, defined as >80% consensus of each criterion. Revisions and additions suggested by participants in Round 1 were incorporated into the Round 2 survey. Round 2 of surveys received responses from 40 of 49 (82%) CHNC sites and again received 100% agreement on criteria.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION(S)
abstract.text: All proposed conditions reached consensus for inclusion, falling into one of three major categories. Consensus-derived criteria for emergent neonatal transport will provide a standardized framework for triage, prioritization and resource utilization. Additionally, these guidelines should facilitate national and international benchmarking, improve efficiency and support neonatal outcome-based research across North America.

articles.title: [Development of a stressor scale for emergency dispatchers in fire service: Reliability and validity assessment].
articles.journal_full: Sangyo eiseigaku zasshi = Journal of occupational health

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Command-and-control operations in fire services are central in disaster response, encompassing emergency call handling and unit deployment management. Previous studies have indicated that emergency call-related duties impose heavy physical and psychological workloads. However, stressors encountered in command-and-control operations in Japanese fire services remain unclear. Therefore, this study identified the components of stressors specific to command-and-control operations in fire services and developed a Stressor Scale for Emergency Dispatchers. The reliability and validity of the scale were examined.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Ten personnel with experience in command-and-control operations in fire services were interviewed regarding work stressors. Accordingly, a preliminary draft of the Stressor Scale for Emergency Dispatchers was created. Subsequently, a questionnaire survey was conducted at participating fire services and firefighting command centers. We surveyed 400 personnel (219 valid responses), whose primary duties involved command-and-control operations in fire services or firefighting command centers. Exploratory factor analysis was implemented to confirm the scale's factor structure. Reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha coefficients, and validity was examined using correlation analyses with related concepts, including occupational stressors, suppression, and stress responses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Exploratory factor analysis revealed that stressors specific to command-and-control operations in fire services involved four factors; "high workload content," "coordination failure," "response to callers," and "difficulty resting." Each factor demonstrated sufficient Cronbach's alpha. Regarding validity, all the factors showed significant positive correlations with occupational stressors and stress responses. Additionally, suppression was only significantly correlated with "response to callers."

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This study clarified the stressors specific to command-and-control operations in fire services. The newly developed Stressor Scale for Emergency Dispatchers was reliable and valid.

articles.title: Work-related electrical injuries in Victoria, Australia: A population-based study of fatalities, hospital attendance and compensation claims.
articles.journal: Aust N Z J Public Health
articles.journal_full: Australian and New Zealand journal of public health

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to describe the frequency, characteristics and burden of work-related electrical injuries in Victoria, Australia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This descriptive epidemiological study used coroner-reported fatalities (July 2018-December 2022), emergency department presentations and hospital admissions (July 2018-June 2024), and workers' compensation claims (July 2018-June 2023). People aged ≥15 years with a work-related electrical injury in the National Coronial Information System, Victorian Emergency Minimum Dataset, Victorian Admitted Episodes Dataset or National Data Set for Compensation-based Statistics were included in the study. Outcomes were annual numbers and rates of work-related electrical injury per 100,000 workers, by age, sex, occupation and industry and injury type.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ten electrical fatalities occurred (<5 work related; exact count suppressed for confidentiality). Between 2018-19 and 2023-24, 2,516 emergency department presentations, 313 hospital admissions and 285 compensation claims were identified (12.1, 1.5 and 1.7 per 100,000 workers, respectively). Rates were highest among males (emergency department: 18.7 per 100,000) and young workers (15-24 years; emergency department: 21.6 per 100,000). Electrotechnology trade workers and labourers were most affected; manufacturing and construction were leading industries.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Work-related electrical injuries remain a preventable hazard, particularly for young men and manual workers.

abstract.label: IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH
abstract.text: Improved surveillance, targeted training and stronger regulation are needed to reduce electrical injury burden.

articles.title: Care under attack: a qualitative study of healthcare system disruption and health worker resilience during airstrikes on Lebanon.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: War severely disrupts healthcare systems by damaging infrastructure, limiting access to care and placing healthcare workers (HCWs) at physical and psychological risk. During the 2024 Israeli war on Lebanon, repeated airstrikes created major challenges for healthcare delivery. This study explored HCWs' experiences and examined the impact of conflict on healthcare system functioning and service continuity.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 19 HCWs involved in emergency response and patient care, including nurses, paramedics and ambulance staff affected during the conflict. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by a critical health systems framework.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Two overarching themes emerged: (1) operational disruption and failures in preparedness and accountability and (2) workforce resilience and professional commitment during crisis. Participants described attacks on healthcare facilities, ambulances and infrastructure that disrupted services, caused shortages of staff and medical supplies and reduced access to care. HCWs described a substantial psychological toll, including fear, anxiety, burnout and emotional exhaustion, alongside moral distress arising from having to weigh patient care against their own safety and from being unable to provide the standard of care they were committed to. Despite these conditions, participants demonstrated resilience through teamwork, rapid adaptation and strong professional dedication, helping sustain essential healthcare services during the conflict.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The findings highlight the vulnerability and resilience of healthcare systems in conflict settings, as well as the considerable psychological and moral burden borne by HCWs. Strengthening emergency preparedness, protecting HCWs and facilities and improving accountability for attacks on healthcare are essential to maintaining healthcare delivery and safeguarding workforce well-being during armed conflict.

articles.title: Beyond Risk Identification: Adherence to a Pediatric Suicide Prevention Pathway in Primary Care.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate adherence to a structured suicide prevention pathway in pediatric primary care and characterize management practices following suicide risk assessment.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study of well-child visits among adolescents aged 12-21 years at an urban academic pediatric clinic from 2022-2024. The pathway incorporated the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 Modified for Adolescents (PHQ-A) for suicide risk identification and the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) for risk assessment. Electronic health record (EHR) data assessed adherence to pathway components, and supplemental chart review characterized management practices, including safety planning and emergency department referral. Multivariable regression examined patient-, provider-, and system-level factors associated with adherence.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 3440 visits, the PHQ-A was completed in 84.8%. Suicide risk was identified in 8.6%, and 57.8% received a C-SSRS. When an EHR alert was triggered, 79% completed the C-SSRS compared with 11% without an alert (p < 0.001). Older adolescents were less likely to receive a C-SSRS assessment (aRR=0.93; 95% CI: 0.89-0.97). Among adolescents with low or moderate C-SSRS risk levels, 20.8% had documentation of a complete six-step collaborative safety plan. Manual chart review identified additional suicide-related management practices beyond the adherence metric, including partial safety planning, behavioral health involvement, referral to mental health services, and ongoing mental health treatment.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Suicide prevention pathways can support identification, assessment, and management of suicide risk in pediatric primary care. EHR-based decision support may improve adherence. Defining evidence-based components of pediatric suicide prevention remains critical.

articles.title: Older Adult Perceptions and Practices Regarding Medication Use and Storage.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Approximately 35,000 young children are brought to US emergency departments annually due to unintentional medication exposures. A 2017 study examining the circumstances surrounding these exposures found that grandparents' medications were involved in 30.7% of prescription and 7.8% of over-the-counter exposures. Therefore, survey data were analyzed to better understand older adult perceptions and practices regarding medication use and storage to help inform interventions to promote safe medication storage behaviors.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Data were collected from February 22, 2024 to February 27, 2024, through an online, "PN View Generation" survey of older adults aged 60 to 78 years.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 986 older adult respondents, 20.8% reported frequent interaction and 79.2% reported infrequent/no interaction with young children. Overall, most respondents (90.8%) reported taking at least one medication/supplement every day. Respondents most commonly reported keeping household medications in a cabinet (56.5%), on a table/desk (30.3%), and on a countertop (20.7%). Nearly half of all older adult respondents (48.5%) reported that they transfer medications from their original bottles to other containers like daily pill organizers/pill boxes. Among respondents who wanted to hear safe medication storage messages (N=769), the most frequently identified locations where they preferred to see/hear messages were at pharmacies (72.7%) and doctors' offices (66.5%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Behaviors that could put young children at risk for unintentional medication exposures were commonly reported. Educational efforts to reach older adults, especially in health care settings, and packaging/storage innovations designed to increase the likelihood that adults keep medications/supplements within child-resistant containers may be necessary to promote safe storage behaviors when spending time with young children.

articles.title: Cardiac paroxysmal orthodeoxia syndrome: A comprehensive process of this challenging disease starting from the clinical suspicion till the therapeutic procedure.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by both dyspnea and arterial desaturation in the upright position that is relieved by returning to a recumbent position. In addition to PFO (as discussed in our case) and other interatrial defects, this syndrome has also been described with intrapulmonary shunting and with disorders such as pericardial effusion, constrictive pericarditis, emphysema, amiodarone pulmonary toxicity, pneumonectomy, and cirrhosis.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We describe a case of platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) due to patent foramen ovale (PFO) occurring during the preoperative evaluation of an elderly patient who presented to the emergency department for a femoral neck fracture. Initial evaluation was shifted to a pulmonary embolism or COVID-19 infection that were excluded by a chest CT with IV contrast and RT-PCR for COVID-19. 12-leads ECG and TTE were unremarkable.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: During hospital stay, the patient complains of positional dyspnoea that develops upon sitting up, accompanied with refractory hypoxaemia that reverts on recumbent position. Following a high clinical suspicion of POS, a bubble contrast echocardiogram was performed and showed important patent foramen ovale (PFO) highlighted by an abundant passage of contrast from the right atrium to the left associated with hyperdynamic interatrial septum. An urgent percutaneous closure was performed, and marked improvement of patient's symptoms has been noted since then.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The diagnosis of POS has been challenging especially during the current pandemic. Our case emphasizes on the importance of a detailed history and physical exam, the role of multimodality imaging techniques to diagnose POS and the high success rate of percutaneous methods for PFO closure.

articles.title: Baseline nutritional-inflammatory status, rather than in-hospital biochemical deterioration, is associated with swallowing recovery in patients with pneumonia: A retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND & AIMS
abstract.text: Dysphagia is common in patients hospitalized for pneumonia and is closely associated with nutritional status. Although poor nutritional status at admission is associated with adverse outcomes, the relationship between short-term in-hospital changes in biochemical nutritional-inflammatory indices and swallowing recovery remains unclear and is difficult to evaluate because such changes are defined using discharge measurements, whereas recovery often occurs earlier. We examined baseline nutritional-inflammatory status as the primary exposure and evaluated longitudinal swallowing trajectories according to eventual in-hospital biochemical deterioration.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective, single-center cohort study included 199 adult patients hospitalized for pneumonia. The Functional Oral Intake Scale (FOIS; range 1-7) was assessed at admission, weekly thereafter, and at discharge. Modified Controlling Nutritional Status (mCONUT; range 0-12) scores were calculated at admission and discharge. The primary exposure was baseline mCONUT, and the primary outcome was time to first achievement of FOIS ≥4. The Cox analysis was restricted to patients with baseline dysphagia (FOIS <4; n = 113, 61 events) and adjusted for baseline covariates. A linear mixed-effects model using repeated FOIS measurements across five timepoints (n = 199 patients, 762 observations) examined whether the rate of FOIS change differed according to eventual mCONUT-worsening status.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Higher baseline mCONUT showed a directionally consistent association with delayed achievement of FOIS ≥4, although the association did not reach conventional statistical significance (adjusted hazard ratio 0.88 per 1-point increase, 95% confidence interval 0.77-1.01, p = 0.068). FOIS improved significantly over time (β = +0.060/day, p < 0.001). Higher baseline mCONUT (β = -0.142, p = 0.036) and greater pre-hospital frailty (β = -0.379, p < 0.001) were associated with lower longitudinal FOIS levels. No significant time × mCONUT-worsening interaction was observed (β = +0.009, p = 0.537), providing no evidence that the rate of FOIS change differed according to eventual in-hospital mCONUT-worsening status.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Higher baseline mCONUT showed a directionally consistent association with delayed swallowing recovery and was associated with lower longitudinal FOIS levels, while greater pre-hospital frailty was also associated with lower FOIS levels over time. No statistically significant difference in the rate of FOIS change was observed according to eventual in-hospital mCONUT-worsening status. Because in-hospital mCONUT change was defined using discharge measurements, associations with early swallowing recovery should be interpreted cautiously owing to temporal-ordering limitations.

articles.title: Impact of Wechat-based prehospital data transmission on reperfusion times in ST-elevation myocardial infarction: a prospective observational study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Early diagnosis of acute ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) is important for the treatment of patients. A Class I evidence demonstrates that every 30-minute delay in PCI is linked to a 7.5% relative increase in 1-year mortality1 "WeChat" is a convenient communication tool that enables the transmission of patient information ‒ including basic details, condition assessments, and relevant laboratory results ‒ to the receiving hospital via WeChat-based transmission. Simultaneously, patients are rapidly transported to the hospital by ambulance for treatment. Thus, the hospital can receive patient information before their arrival, thereby significantly reducing diagnosis and treatment time. This integrated model is collectively referred to as WeChat-based transmission. Therefore, the early activation of WeChat-based emergency medical services transmission plays a critical role in improving patient prognosis. The present study sought to investigate the use of WeChat-based transmission in patients with acute STEMI.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: 409 eligible STEMI patients (May 2022-November 2024) were grouped by WeChat-based transmission use: 96 in the observation group and 313 in the control group. Baseline data, medical history, and key times (S-to-FMC, d-to-B, TIT) were compared. Factors influencing WeChat-based transmission use were analyzed via SPSS 22.0 (p < 0.05 significant).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 96 (23.4%) patients in the WeChat-based transmission group and 313 (76.6%) patients in the N-WeChat group were enrolled. S‑to‑FMC time was associated with lower median values in the WeChat‑based transmission group (median 75 vs. 120 minutes, p < 0.05); similar patterns were seen for D‑to‑B time (50 vs. 67 minutes, p < 0.05) and total ischemia time (121.5 vs. 150.0 minutes, p < 0.05). Shorter time to Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) diagnosis, as well as shorter D‑to‑B and TIT times, were observed among patients in the WeChat‑based transmission group relative to patients in the non‑WeChat‑based transmission group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: WeChat-based transmission was associated with shorter S-to-FMC, d-to-B, and TIT times during patient transfer for PCI. However, it is not fully used for transporting chest pain patients in and around Shijiazhuang City. Therefore, strengthening WeChat-based transmission function in public education of pre-hospital rescue remains the focus of our future work.

articles.title: Differences in Prehospital Assessment by Language Barrier Among Blunt Trauma Patients: A National Emergency Medical Services Study.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Language barriers may impede Emergency Medical Services (EMS) evaluation and treatment of trauma patients, potentially leading to misdiagnosis and poorer outcomes. We examined whether patient-provider language barriers were associated with differences in prehospital evaluation and management of blunt trauma patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective review of EMS activations was conducted using the ImageTrend Collaborate dataset. Blunt trauma patients evaluated by EMS nationwide from 2022 to 2023 were included. Data were categorized into language barrier (LB) and no language barrier (NLB) groups, with LB defined as cases where EMS providers documented an LB with the patient. Univariate and bivariate analyses were conducted using Stata, version 19.0.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1,220,982 blunt trauma patients, 24,857 (2%) had a documented LB. LB patients were more likely to be male (53.5% versus 47.4%, P < 0.05), younger (44 versus 58 mean age, P < 0.05), and Hispanic (58.9% versus 7.6%). LB patients were more frequently injured in motor vehicle collisions (25.6% versus 17.1%, P < 0.05), whereas NLB patients were most frequently injured in falls (29.5% versus 19.9%, P < 0.05). A slightly greater proportion of LB patients presented with low Glasgow Coma Scale scores (3-8) compared with NLB patients (5.2% versus 4.2%, P < 0.05). LB patients were more likely to be treated and transported to the hospital (80.3% versus 75.1%, P < 0.05) and less likely to have pain scores documented (60.6% versus 63.6%, P < 0.05). The mean on-scene time was similar between groups (17.0 versus 17.4 min).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Patient-provider LBs in blunt trauma patients were associated with differences in demographic characteristics, injury mechanisms, and prehospital assessment patterns. Further research is needed to better characterize associations between LBs and trauma care and to improve standardized reporting practices.

articles.title: Defining Rotational Thromboelastometry Thresholds for Fibrinolysis Phenotyping and Massive Transfusion Prediction in Trauma.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Fibrinolysis, or clot breakdown, is a major contributor to death in severely injured patients. Thromboelastography (TEG) has established cutoffs for fibrinolysis phenotypes, hyperfibrinolysis, physiologic fibrinolysis, and fibrinolytic shutdown, but analogous thresholds for rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) remain limited. This study aimed to characterize fibrinolysis phenotypes using ROTEM and identify predictors of massive transfusion (MT) in trauma patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Among 2474 trauma patients who underwent ROTEM testing at an adult level I trauma center from 2018 to 2024, 2257 had an available EXTEM maximum lysis (ML) value and were included in the fibrinolysis phenotype analysis. Patients were categorized by EXTEM ML: shutdown (ML < 3%), physiologic (ML 3-15%), or hyperfibrinolysis (ML > 15%). The primary outcome was MT within 4 h; secondary outcomes included 24-h transfusion requirements, length of stay, and mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The median age was 46 y; 70.9% were male, and the median Injury Severity Score was 24.3. Hyperfibrinolysis occurred in 5.3% (n = 119), physiologic fibrinolysis in 64.6% (n = 1458), and shutdown in 30.1% (n = 680). Mortality was highest in hyperfibrinolysis (58.0%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 49.0-66.5%) versus physiologic (10.6%; 95% CI: 9.2-12.3%) and shutdown (20.4%; 95% CI: 17.6-23.6%) (P < 0.001). MT within 4 h was 37.0% (95% CI: 28.8-45.9%) in hyperfibrinolysis versus 6.9% (95% CI: 5.7-8.3%) and 11.3% (95% CI: 9.2-13.9%), respectively.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This study externally validates previously described ROTEM-specific EXTEM ML thresholds for fibrinolysis phenotyping in an independent trauma cohort. Hyperfibrinolysis strongly predicted MT and was associated with high mortality, whereas shutdown identified a distinct high-risk group. These findings support integration of ROTEM-specific fibrinolysis criteria into trauma protocols and prospective evaluation of phenotype-directed resuscitation strategies.

articles.title: Age-Friendly Design and Optimization of Digital Health Technologies for Medication Adherence in Older Adults With Chronic Diseases: Scoping Review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Medication nonadherence represents a persistent clinical challenge among older adults with chronic diseases, complicating long-term disease management and prognosis. Digital health technologies (DHTs) deliver promising opportunities for remote, out-of-hospital medication management; nevertheless, age-related cognitive-physiological decline and insufficient digital literacy widen the digital divide, creating barriers to real-world uptake and sustained use of DHTs. Existing systematic reviews mainly synthesize intervention effect sizes, but few unpack multilevel drivers of mixed outcomes or generate actionable age-friendly design guidance that is empirically grounded and tailored to older adult needs.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This scoping review aimed to identify and characterize DHT interventions designed to improve medication adherence in older adults with chronic diseases, examine the range of factors influencing their use, and derive age-friendly design principles from the available literature.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Following the scoping review framework by Arksey and O'Malley and the PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, we searched 7 databases from January 1, 2013, to August 2026. An updated search was performed on September 2, 2026, to ensure the currency of the studies. Eligible sources included quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods original studies as well as secondary reviews published in English or Chinese. Two independent reviewers performed screening, data extraction, and thematic synthesis guided by social cognitive theory and person-environment fit theory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 60 studies were included, of which 46 (76.7%) were published between 2022 and August 2026, indicating rapidly growing research interest. Study mapping revealed a skewed distribution across the medication journey, with most investigations concentrated on the daily routine phase, while prescription, pickup, storage, and refill remained severely understudied. We synthesized a 4-level model comprising individual, technical, social-environmental, and intervention program factors influencing DHT performance. Major study gaps were identified: only 1 study specifically recruited older adults living alone, only 1 study used validated standardized usability metrics, and no included study assessed bidirectional electronic health record interoperability. Based on barriers reported by older users, we derived a 5-dimension age-friendly design framework encompassing perceptibility, comprehensibility, operability, emotional warmth, and security-interoperability.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Moving beyond prior reviews focused predominantly on intervention efficacy, this scoping review presents a theory-informed 4-level influencing-factor model and an empirically derived age-friendly design framework to guide future development and implementation. For clinical practice, nurses and other health care professionals should conduct preimplementation baseline assessments of older adults' cognitive function, digital literacy, and social support and tailor DHT recommendations accordingly. For future research, investigators should prioritize socially vulnerable subgroups, including those living alone and those in resource-limited settings, standardize usability reporting using validated instruments, and actively integrate clinical system interoperability to enable closed-loop care. Closing intra-age-group digital health inequities requires interdisciplinary collaboration across nursing, medicine, pharmacy, and health informatics, ensuring that DHTs become tools of empowerment rather than sources of exclusion.

articles.title: Feasibility and Acceptability of Oura Ring Sleep Monitoring in Older Adults Admitted From the Emergency Department: Prospective Cohort Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) boarding exposes admitted older adults to a high-disruption environment. Sleep loss during acute hospitalization is associated with adverse outcomes and may contribute to delirium, yet objective sleep measurement in this setting is difficult. Consumer multisensor wearables may permit low-burden, longitudinal measurement, but the feasibility and acceptability of ring-based monitoring among acutely ill older adults is unknown.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to estimate the feasibility and acceptability of Oura Ring Gen 3 sleep monitoring in older adults admitted to the hospital from the ED, and to describe exploratory device-measured and patient-reported sleep outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-site prospective cohort study from February through March 2025. Patients aged 65 years or older with an inpatient medical bed request were recruited in the ED and asked to wear the ring continuously for up to 4 days or until discharge; monitoring continued after transfer to an inpatient unit from the ED. Participants underwent daily 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for Confusion Assessment Method-Defined Delirium (3D-CAM) assessments, cognitive testing when not delirious, daily sleep surveys, and an exit survey. Feasibility outcomes were the approached-to-enrolled proportion and the proportion of study completers with wear for more than 75% of the analyzed period. Acceptability was the proportion of exit respondents who disagreed or strongly disagreed that the ring bothered them. Device-estimated sleep duration was normalized to hours per 24 hours, and its association with mean patient-reported sleep quality was assessed using Kendall τ.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 29 patients approached for consent, 15 enrolled (51.7%, 95% CI 32.5%-70.6%); 1 withdrew immediately, leaving 14 who completed study procedures. Of these 14 patients, 13 wore the ring for ≥75% of their enrollment period (92.9%, 95% CI 66.1%-99.8%). Eleven participants completed the exit survey, and 9 reported that the ring was not bothersome (81.8%, 95% CI 48.2%-97.7%). Among the 13 participants who wore the ring for ≥75% of the analyzed period, median device-estimated sleep was 4.3 (IQR 2.6-7.0) hours per 24 hours. Participants reported good or very good sleep on 9 of 19 surveyed nights (47.4%). Mean sleep quality and device-estimated sleep duration were positively associated among 10 participants with complete paired data (Kendall τ=0.54; P=.04).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this pilot study, we found that sleep monitoring with the Oura Ring Gen 3 was feasible and acceptable to older adults admitted from the ED. These findings support larger studies validating the Oura Ring against polysomnography in hospitalized older adults.

articles.title: Craniofacial Injuries in International Football: From Return to Play to Prevention.
Oral vs Intravenous Fluid Therapy in Emergency Department Patients: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Feasibility and Noninferiority Trial.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Intravenous fluid therapy is widely used in emergency departments (EDs) to treat hypovolemia and hypotension. However, its hemodynamic effects are often modest and short-lived. Intravenous fluid therapy requires a peripheral venous catheter, which increases the risk of complications such as catheter failure and phlebitis. Oral fluid therapy represents a simple, noninvasive alternative that has been shown in physiological studies to expand plasma volume and increase blood pressure. No randomized trial has compared oral with intravenous fluid therapy in a general adult ED population. Evidence regarding the feasibility of randomized comparisons of fluid administration modes and whether oral fluid administration can reliably deliver the prescribed volume remains limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial of oral vs intravenous fluid therapy in ED patients requiring fluid replacement and to determine whether oral fluid therapy is noninferior to intravenous fluid therapy in achieving the prescribed fluid volume.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This investigator-initiated, multicenter, open-label randomized controlled feasibility and noninferiority trial will enroll 250 adult ED patients prescribed ≥1000 mL of intravenous crystalloid therapy. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either oral fluids or intravenous crystalloid. The primary feasibility outcome is protocol adherence, defined as the proportion of randomized participants who receive the allocated route of administration without a major protocol deviation. The primary clinical outcome is the proportion of patients achieving the prescribed fluid volume during the ED stay, censored at 48 hours after randomization and analyzed using a noninferiority framework. Noninferiority of oral fluid therapy will be tested against the null hypothesis that the intravenous proportion exceeds the oral proportion by at least the noninferiority margin of 15 percentage points, using the difference in proportions with a 1-sided 97.5% CI (equivalent to a 2-sided 95% CI) from an exact proportion test. The sample size of 250 will provide 90% power at a 1-sided α of .025 under an assumed proportion of 85% in both arms.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The study was funded by the Region of Southern Denmark in May 2024. Recruitment began in October 2025 at 3 Danish EDs, and 85 participants have been recruited as of September 2026. Recruitment is projected to close in October 2026, with final 30-day follow-up projected for November 2026. No amendments to the protocol have been made. Results are expected to be published in summer 2027.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This trial will evaluate whether a randomized trial comparing intravenous and oral fluid therapy is feasible in ED patients and whether oral fluid therapy can achieve prescribed fluid volumes comparable to those achieved with intravenous therapy. The findings will inform the design of a future definitive effectiveness trial.

articles.title: Two-year follow-up of postcommercialisation cohort of 100 bridge-enhanced anterior cruciate ligament restorations shows low retear rate and good patient-reported outcomes.
articles.journal_full: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To review adverse events and outcomes 2 years postoperatively from the Bridge Enhanced anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) Restoration (BEAR) procedure in the first 100 subjects of the Bridge registry, a postcommercialisation prospective cohort.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Technique modifications (repair and bridging suture type, femoral and tibial fixation), adverse events and reoperations were recorded. Physical examinations were reported at 0, 6, 9 and 12 months and patient-reported outcomes (International Knee Documentation Committee, knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score, Marx, return to sport index) were reported at 0, 6, 9, 12 and 24 months. Adverse events were compared between the original and modified technique groups using Fisher's Exact test. Paired t-tests were used to compare patient-reported outcomes at 1 and 2 years.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean follow-up was 22.3 ± 5.5 months, range 3-32.7 months, with five subjects exiting early. Mean age was 31.8 ± 14.3 years (range 7.7-69.6). Sixty-seven per cent were female. Fifty-five underwent a BEAR procedure using the original technique, while 45 had a modified surgical technique. The overall rates of adverse events with reoperations at 2 years included: two ACL retears with meniscus injury, two ACL retears without meniscus injury, two contralateral tears, five meniscus injuries without ACL retear (one medial, three lateral, one both medial and lateral), two manipulations under anaesthesia, one lysis of adhesions/cyclops removal and four removals of retained suture. Overall reoperation rate was 18.9% (17/90) at 2 years (28.0% with original technique, 7.5% with modified technique; p = 0.02) with 5.6% (5/90) ipsilateral ACL retear rate. There were no significant differences in ACL retear rates between the original technique and modified technique groups. From 1 to 2 years, there were statistically significant improvements in IKDC and three of the five KOOS scales.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The rates of ACL retear status post BEAR with and without modification are low at 2 years, with five retears occurring between 14 and 28 months. Excellent stability and range of motion are attained at 1 year, with good patient reported outcomes measures at 2 years.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level II, cohort study.

articles.title: Two-dimensional shear wave elastography-based assessment of liver stiffness in critically ill patients with septic shock: a prospective observational study.

abstract.text: The acute effects of resuscitation on the liver during septic shock, as assessed through liver stiffness, are not well understood. The objective of this pilot study was to evaluate liver stiffness in patients with septic shock using two-dimensional shear wave elastography (2D-SWE). This prospective study was conducted at a 30-bed ICU of a university hospital. Patients with septic shock, who had apparently normal liver status before current illness, requiring vasopressors for ≥ 24 h were considered within 7 days after the onset of shock. Patients with pre-existing liver diseases, congestive heart failure, intra-abdominal hypertension, recent history of abdominal trauma/surgery, body mass index ≥ 35 kg/m2, and pregnancy were excluded. Liver stiffness was measured by 2D-SWE scan, which was repeated after at least 4 weeks of recovery from shock. Fifty-two patients aged 44 (34-63) years in septic shock with median SOFA score 9 (IQR 6-11) were included. The median liver stiffness after the onset of septic shock was 30 kPa (IQR 25.2-34.2), a significantly higher than normal value (< 7 kPa). This stiffness was significantly associated with vasoactive dose index (VDI) [linear regression coefficient (β): 23.02; 95%CI 16.60-29.69; p = 0.001]. The limited follow-up measurements (in 18 survivors) revealed a marked reduction in liver stiffness values from 29 kPa (IQR 26-32) to 6 kPa (IQR 5.4-6.4). Assessment of liver through 2D-SWE, after the onset of septic shock in apparently normal liver status pre-illness, revealed increased stiffness. However, it reverted to normal once clinical condition improved. Clinical Trials Registry - India: CTRI/2023/06/053891.

articles.title: A Return to Performance Continuum for Football (Soccer) Players After ACL Reconstruction: Bridging Rehabilitation, Return to Play and Sustained Performance.

abstract.text: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in football (soccer) players is associated with high return-to-competition rates but persistent deficits in performance and elevated risk of secondary injury. Whilst rehabilitation frameworks have evolved to optimise early, mid-, and late-stage recovery, limited guidance exists regarding the structured transition from typical return-to-sport clearance to sustained return-to-performance (RTPerf). Failure to adequately bridge this gap may contribute to early re-injury, suppressed match performance and compromised career longevity. This paper outlines a staged RTPerf continuum comprising: (1) structured on-field rehabilitation, (2) return to team training, (3) return to competitive match play and (4) early and sustained RTPerf. Four interdependent pillars underpin this process: (i) the restoration of movement quality under realistic football specific situations; (ii) progressive football-specific technical and tactical re-training; (iii) football-specific physical reconditioning including speed, acceleration, deceleration and change of direction ability, endurance and chronic workload development and (iv) maximal strength and explosive neuromuscular performance restoration.

articles.title: Perioperative NSAID use and postoperative outcomes after distal radius fracture surgery: a propensity-matched cohort study.
articles.journal_full: European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie

abstract.label: PURPOSE
