Craving reduction was significantly greater in the rTMS group than in the TAU group from baseline to 1 month (4.0 vs 0.5, p < 0.001) and from baseline to 3 months (4.0 vs 1.5, p < 0.001) but not from baseline to 6 months (3.50 vs 2.50, p = 0.217). Substance use frequency significantly decreased from baseline to 1, 3, and 6 months in both groups (all p < 0.001). The rTMS group had fewer accident and emergency department admissions, fewer psychiatric admissions, and fewer days of psychiatric admission. No rTMS-related adverse effects were reported. In the TAU group, lower baseline craving predicted a higher likelihood of 1-month abstinence and remained significant after adjustment (odds ratio = 0.659, p = 0.018). In the rTMS group, antidepressant use predicted a lower likelihood of 1-month abstinence and remained significant after adjustment (odds ratio = 0.211, p = 0.041). Allocation to the rTMS group predicted greater craving reduction at 1 month (β = 3.140, p < 0.001) and at 3 months (β = 2.089, p = 0.001). More previous psychiatric admissions (β = -0.308, p = 0.039) and receipt of rTMS in an inpatient setting (β = -1.944, p = 0.041) predicted smaller craving reductions at 3 months.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Adjunctive rTMS was associated with greater craving reduction at 1 and 3 months but did not significantly shorten the time to achieve 1-month abstinence. Higher baseline craving in the TAU group and antidepressant use in the rTMS group were associated with a lower likelihood of achieving 1-month abstinence.

articles.title: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on long-term trends in psychiatric service utilisation at an accident and emergency department in Hong Kong.
articles.journal_full: East Asian archives of psychiatry : official journal of the Hong Kong College of Psychiatrists = Dong Ya jing shen ke xue zhi : Xianggang jing shen ke yi xue yuan qi kan

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To describe trends in psychiatric service utilisation at the accident and emergency department (AED) of the Prince of Wales Hospital, Hong Kong, between July 2017 and June 2024.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective observational study reviewed medical records of patients who received psychiatric services in the AED of the Prince of Wales Hospital, Hong Kong, between July 2017 and June 2024 encompassing periods before the pandemic (July 2017 to December 2019), during the pandemic (January 2020 to September 2022), and after the pandemic (October 2022 to June 2024). The 'window period' (May 2021 to December 2021), during which no community outbreak was reported, was excluded from the pandemic period. Data collected included patient demographics, psychiatric diagnoses, and management plans. Trends in psychiatric service utilisation during the study period were analysed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In total, 7441 AED psychiatric consultations (61.1% women) were included in the analysis. The median patient age significantly increased from 45 years in 2017 to 49 years in 2024 (p = 0.007). There was an increasing trend in AED psychiatric service utilisation. Attendance counts decreased during the first two quarters of 2020 (beginning of the pandemic) and substantially surged in 2021 during the window period, followed by a sharp decline in 2022 during the fifth wave driven by the Omicron variant and then rebounded at the beginning of 2023, and the upward trend continued. Daily attendance counts significantly increased from 2017 to 2024 among patients with major neurocognitive disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, and disorders specifically associated with stress. Discharge to the community was the most common management plan.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted access to healthcare services in patients with psychiatric illnesses. Demand for AED psychiatric services rebounded after the pandemic. Between 2017 and 2024, the overall patient age increased, and service utilisation increased among patients with major neurocognitive disorders and neurodevelopmental disorders.

articles.title: Effects of an online stroke education program on enhancing knowledge, awareness of stroke warning signs, and emergency medical services seeking among high-risk residents in Huanggang City, China.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education and health promotion

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Stroke is the leading cause of disability and death in china. Raising public awareness of warning signs is critical for improving access to emergency services and treatment outcomes. Prehospital delay remains a significant challenge, especially among high-risk populations. This study therefore aims to determine the effects of an online stroke education program (osp) on the knowledge, awareness of stroke warning signs, and seeking of emergency medical services (ems) among high-risk residents.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from September 2024 to April 2025. One hundred and six high-risk residents were randomly allocated to intervention and control groups (n = 53 each). The intervention group received the 6-week OSP program, while the control group received regular health education. Data were collected via an interview questionnaire and analyzed using the Chi-squared test, McNemar's test, and multivariate regression.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Postintervention, the experimental group exhibited significantly higher enhancement of stroke-related knowledge, awareness of warning signs, and EMS-seeking behavior compared to the control group (P < 0.05). The intervention effects were robust, showing significant improvements in awareness (adjusted OR = 3.78, 95% CI: 1.41-8.13), knowledge (adjusted OR = 3.68, 95% CI: 1.52-8.94), and EMS seeking (adjusted OR = 3.33, 95% CI: 1.44-7.69).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The OSP significantly improved stroke recognition and EMS-seeking intentions. This scalable model supports stroke care management by integrating digital education into primary care, effectively reducing prehospital delays. Such integration is crucial for improving clinical outcomes in acute stroke management and achieving public health targets.

articles.title: Comparing the pain relief effectiveness of intravenous magnesium sulfate and ketorolac versus intravenous morphine and ketorolac for kidney stones.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education and health promotion

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pain is one of the most common symptoms in various diseases. While morphine is widely used for pain relief, its adverse effects and potential for misuse have led to the exploration of safer alternatives. This study aimed to compare the analgesic effectiveness of intravenous magnesium sulfate versus morphine, both in combination with ketorolac, in patients with renal colic.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: In this double-blind randomized controlled trial, 174 patients with renal colic referred to the emergency department of Shahid Ganjiyan Hospital in Dezful were enrolled. Patients were randomly allocated into two equal groups (n = 87). The intervention group received intravenous magnesium sulfate (50 mg/kg diluted in 100 mL normal saline over 15 minutes) plus ketorolac (30 mg), while the control group received intravenous morphine (0.1 mg/kg) plus ketorolac (30 mg). Pain intensity was measured using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at baseline (admission), and 20, 40, and 60 minutes after drug administration. Demographic data were also collected.

abstract.label: RESULT
abstract.text: Among the 174 participants included in the study, 65% were male and aged between 40 and 60 years. Statistical tests indicated no significant differences between the two groups concerning demographic characteristics. Thus, the groups are comparable in terms of demographic variables. Comparison of pain reduction between the two groups at different time points revealed no statistically significant difference. The mean pain scores decreased over time in both groups; however, the differences between the groups were not significant at 20 minutes (P = 0.45), 40 minutes (P = 0.74), or 60 minutes post-intervention (P = 0.65). These findings indicate that both treatment protocols (morphine plus ketorolac and magnesium sulfate plus ketorolac) had similar effects on pain reduction at all measured intervals.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The findings of this study demonstrate that intravenous magnesium sulfate, in combination with ketorolac, is as effective as morphine-based regimens in managing acute renal colic pain. Given the current global health policies emphasizing opioid stewardship and the reduction of opioid-related adverse effects, magnesium sulfate emerges as a valuable, low-risk alternative. Its incorporation into emergency pain management protocols may not only reduce opioid dependency and misuse but also align with broader public health goals aimed at promoting safer and more sustainable pain relief strategies. Health policymakers should consider including non-opioid analgesics like magnesium sulfate in national and institutional guidelines for acute pain management, especially in settings where opioid overuse presents a clinical and social challenge.

articles.title: Enhancing first-aid self-efficacy: A randomized trial comparing three interactive educational ınterventions.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education and health promotion

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Effective first-aid education is a critical public health strategy to reduce the burden on emergency services. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of three interactive first-aid training modalities (case-, video-, and drama-based) on university students' first-aid self-efficacy.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: A three-arm randomized controlled trial with a pretest-post-test design was conducted. The study included 93 university students, randomly assigned to three intervention groups (n = 31 each). The intervention groups received six core first-aid topics delivered through case-, video-, or drama-based methods, while the control group received unstructured education. Data were collected using the "First Aid Self-Efficacy Scale." Statistical analysis was performed using analysis of covariance to compare post-test scores while controlling for baseline differences.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: More than 95% of the participants were unmarried, and more than 50% in each study group were female. Post-test mean scale scores were highest in the case-based group (194.16 ± 25.17), followed by the video-based (190.61 ± 24.08), drama-based (168.22 ± 54.37), and unstructured groups (162.29 ± 45.19). Baseline sociodemographic assessments revealed a statistically significant difference in gender distribution across groups (p = 0.008). However, after adjusting for these baseline scores, the study results showed no statistically significant differences between the three interactive training groups in total first-aid self-efficacy or its subdimensions at post-test (p > 0.050). While all groups demonstrated a longitudinal improvement in self-efficacy scores from preintervention to postintervention, no single interactive method demonstrated statistical superiority over the others.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Interactive first-aid training, regardless of the specific modality, is effective in enhancing students' self-efficacy. These findings suggest that educators can flexibly employ a range of interactive strategies to achieve comparable outcomes in prehospital emergency care training. Interactive first-aid training meets essential health policy benchmarks for emergency preparedness, offering educators flexible, effective, and interchangeable modalities to enhance public self-efficacy.

articles.title: Examination of students' perspectives regarding the effectiveness of clinical training: A research endeavor congruent with social responsibility.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education and health promotion

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Clinical education is a fundamental component of medical training. This study examines the experiences of clinical students across various health professions to provide valuable insights for educational planners involved in designing effective and socially relevant clinical training curricula.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This descriptive-analytical study employed a stratified random sampling method to select clinical students from the disciplines of nursing, midwifery, operating room technology, and pre-hospital emergency medicine at educational institutions in Shoushtar. Data were gathered using a standardized questionnaire designed to evaluate factors affecting the quality of clinical education. The data were analyzed using Pearson correlation, Chi-square tests, independent t-tests, and analysis of variance (ANOVA).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 190 students participated in the study, including 60 males and 130 females, with ages ranging from 18 to 39 years. Participants were enrolled in nursing (n = 105), operating room technology (n = 30), midwifery (n = 40), and emergency medicine (n = 15) programs. Male students reported significantly lower scores in areas related to student-teacher interactions, the learning environment, and evaluation criteria. Notably, overall clinical education scores demonstrated a decreasing trend with increasing age. Emergency medicine students achieved the highest scores, while those in nursing and operating room programs recorded the lowest.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The mean scores related to educational objectives, instructor quality, student-teacher interactions, and the learning environment were lower among male students, older participants, and those enrolled in nursing and operating room programs. These findings highlight the need for targeted educational interventions to improve clinical training objectives, enhance the involvement of qualified instructors, and foster more supportive learning environments.

articles.title: Achilles Tendon Rupture Following Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy for Chronic Tendinopathy Despite Symptomatic Resolution: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) is widely used in the management of chronic Achilles tendinopathy (AT) and is associated with improved pain and functional outcomes. However, symptomatic recovery may not necessarily reflect restoration of tendon structural integrity or mechanical resilience. We report the case of a 61-year-old active male with a ten-year history of chronic mid-portion AT refractory to conservative management who underwent six sessions of radial ESWT, resulting in complete pain resolution and return to unrestricted sporting activity. Six months after completing treatment, he sustained an acute Achilles tendon rupture following a low-energy mechanism while stepping off a pavement. Clinical examination and point-of-care ultrasound confirmed tendon discontinuity with apposable tendon ends. The patient underwent non-operative management with equinus immobilization and progressive rehabilitation. Follow-up ultrasound demonstrated partial tendon healing, although persistent pain and functional limitation remained at the latest follow-up. This case highlights the potential dissociation between symptomatic improvement and structural tendon recovery in chronic AT. Although no causal relationship between ESWT and tendon rupture can be inferred, symptomatic improvement may permit return to higher loading demands despite persistent underlying tendon degeneration. Clinicians should recognize that symptom resolution does not necessarily indicate restoration of tendon mechanical resilience and should consider appropriate counseling and graduated return-to-loading strategies following successful ESWT.

articles.title: Emergency Critical Care as a Continuum: The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Three-Tiered Framework for the Assessment and Management of Critically Ill Patients in the Emergency Department.

abstract.text: Emergency critical care (ECC) is increasingly recognized as an indispensable component of the critical care continuum, beginning at the point of first medical contact in the emergency department (ED). As critically ill patients spend longer periods in the ED and emergency physicians assume an expanding role in providing ongoing critical care, existing assessment frameworks may not fully address the evolving cognitive demands of ECC. This article describes a conceptual three-tier framework intended to provide a pragmatic strategy for the assessment and management of critically ill patients throughout their ED course. The framework was conceived and implemented at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Rishikesh. The framework aligns patient assessment and management with three complementary clinical priorities. Tier 1 emphasizes physiological rescue through simultaneous assessment and stabilization using an expanded ABCDEF approach, with a focus on identifying and managing immediately life-threatening and time-sensitive conditions. Following initial stabilization, Tier 2 focuses on diagnostic reasoning, integrating clinical evaluation to establish an ED working diagnosis and guide subsequent management. Tier 3 addresses longitudinal ECC through structured reassessment, optimization of organ support, diagnostic refinement, and prevention of secondary complications while patients remain under ED care. Although presented as three sequential tiers for conceptual clarity, the framework is intended to be dynamic and iterative, allowing movement between tiers according to the patient's evolving clinical status. By integrating principles of emergency medicine and critical care, this conceptual framework provides a cognitive scaffold for clinicians managing critically ill patients in the ED and may support continuity of care, education, and quality improvement. As the framework is currently conceptual, further studies are required to evaluate its feasibility and potential impact on patient outcomes.

articles.title: Muscle or Subcutaneous Fat? A Prospective Ultrasonographic Study of Dorsogluteal Injection Accuracy in the Emergency Department.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Dorsogluteal intramuscular (i.m.) injection is commonly used in emergency departments, but successful delivery into muscle tissue may vary depending on patient anatomy.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of dorsogluteal i.m. injections performed in the emergency department using immediate postinjection ultrasonography and to identify factors associated with successful i.m. deposition.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective observational study was conducted in the dedicated injection area of a tertiary care emergency department between June 1 and June 15, 2018. Adult patients receiving dorsogluteal i.m. injections were consecutively enrolled. After exclusions, 134 patients were included in the study. The primary outcome was ultrasonographic determination of whether the injectate was deposited in the i.m. or subcutaneous (s.c.) plane. To address interobserver reliability, 20 additional consecutive patients receiving injections underwent independent ultrasonographic assessment by both radiologists, each blinded to the other radiologist's classification. Agreement was summarized using overall percentage agreement and Cohen's κ with a 95% confidence interval (CI), where estimable.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 134 patients, 72 (53.7%) were men. Ultrasonography reported that 82 injections (61.2%) reached the i.m. plane, whereas 52 (38.8%) remained in the s.c. tissue. Successful i.m. deposition was significantly more frequent in men than in women (88.9% vs. 29.0%, p < 0.001). s.c. tissue thickness and combined skin-plus-s.c. tissue thickness reported stronger discrimination for s.c. deposition than body mass index (BMI). In the additional 20-patient dual-ultrasound reliability cohort, the radiologists agreed on the clinically dichotomized injection outcome (correct i.m. vs. incorrect s.c./s.c.-i.m. deposition) in 19 of 20 examinations (95.0%), with a Cohen's κ of 0.875 (95% CI, 0.638-1.000), indicating almost perfect agreement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A considerable proportion of dorsogluteal injections performed in the emergency department do not reach the target muscle tissue. Direct regional s.c. tissue thickness seems to be a more clinically informative determinant of injection success than BMI alone.

articles.title: Impact of Emergency Department Point-of-Care Ultrasound on the Emergency Department Length of Stay and Time to Diagnosis in Early Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early pregnancy complications represent a substantial reason for emergency department (ED) visits, with ectopic pregnancy remaining a significant cause of maternal mortality.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the effectiveness of ED point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) vs. standard radiology- or obstetric-performed ultrasound (US) for early pregnancy assessment in emergency settings.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Four databases were systematically searched for studies including patients with early pregnancy (<20 weeks of gestation) presenting to the ED. Differences in ED length of stay (LOS), time to diagnosis, time to surgery for patients with ectopic pregnancy, and the rate of missed ectopic cases were analyzed. Weighted mean differences (WMDs) and risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews database (ID CRD420251242734).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirteen studies with 4057 early pregnancy patients (ED POCUS = 1848 and standard US = 2209) were included. Compared with standard imaging, ED POCUS was associated with statistically significant reductions in ED LOS (WMD -59.53, 95% CI -77.43 to -41.62, p < 0.00001) and time to definitive diagnosis (WMD -80.93, 95% CI -119.10 to -42.77, p < 0.0001). Moreover, pooled analysis reported no statistically significant difference in the rate of missed ectopic cases between ED POCUS and standard US (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.39-3.87, p = 0.73).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: ED POCUS is associated with measurable improvements in emergency care efficiency without a statistically significant increase in missed diagnoses of ectopic pregnancy. Future high-quality, multicenter randomized studies are needed to better define the diagnostic accuracy, safety, and generalizability of ED POCUS in early pregnancy evaluation.

articles.title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of Mock American Board of Emergency Medicine Ultrasound Cases for Emergency Medicine Residents.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The maturation of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) within the specialty of Emergency Medicine (EM) has led to its incorporation into the newest iteration of the American Board of Emergency Medicine (ABEM) Certifying Examination. The new iteration of the exam will consist of ultrasound cases that will include at least two image acquisition and two interpretation components. Examinees will be asked to acquire and interpret ultrasound images on a standardized patient. The objective of this study was to evaluate resident performance and confidence during a two-case mock ultrasound curriculum designed to familiarize trainees with the ultrasound component of the ABEM Certifying Examination.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This is a single blinded, cross-over study at the University of Arizona College of Medicine (Tucson, Arizona, United States). The study participants were EM resident physicians. A panel of POCUS experts developed two mock cases modeled after the ABEM certification ultrasound case. Residents were randomly assigned to a cardiac or thoracic-based case. Prior to participation, they were asked to independently watch the ABEM instructional video. They underwent an examination with a standardized patient, proctored by POCUS experts. After a one-month interval, participants were assessed on the alternate case. Data were collected from January 1, 2025 to May 1, 2026.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 64 EM residents participated in the study. 48 completed the cross-over design, and 16 completed one day of the examination. Those that did review the material scored higher with a median score of 14 compared to 13, however, this was not statistically significant (p-value of 0.36). On Day 1, the mean overall score (out of 15) was 11.96 ± 2.49 for the Cardiac group and 11.62 ± 1.92 for the Pulmonary group. On Day 2, the mean overall scores increased to 12.55 ± 2.45 and 12.75 ± 2.24, respectively. There was no significant difference in mean scores between the Cardiac and Pulmonary cases on either Day 1 (p=0.57) or Day 2 (p=0.74). When comparing performance across days within each case type, Pulmonary case scores demonstrated a statistically significant increase from Day 1 to Day 2 (p=0.05). Across all participants on Day 1, post-graduate year (PGY) level was moderately correlated with total score (r=0.45, p=0.0007), with more senior residents tending to achieve higher examination scores.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A focused, two-case preparatory curriculum was feasible across multiple residency programs and associated with differences in performance across testing days, particularly in the pulmonary ultrasound scenarios. Early exposure to mock examination cases may help residents develop familiarity with the observed structured clinical examination (OSCE)-style interface, strengthen technical and communication skills, and improve readiness for board certification.

articles.title: Knowledge and Awareness of Myocardial Infarction Symptoms and Appropriate Emergency Response Among the General Adult Population in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study.

abstract.text: Background and objective Delayed recognition of myocardial infarction (MI) symptoms is a preventable driver of cardiovascular mortality, yet the extent to which the public in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, can identify these symptoms and respond appropriately in an emergency has not been well studied. This study aimed to assess awareness of MI symptoms and the appropriate emergency response among adults in Jeddah, and to determine which sociodemographic and health-related factors are associated with this awareness. Methods In this descriptive cross-sectional study, 281 adults aged 18 years and older in Jeddah completed a self-administered online questionnaire covering sociodemographic and health-related characteristics, recognition of six typical and atypical MI symptoms (yielding an awareness score ranging from 0 to 6), and knowledge of the correct emergency response. Correct recognition of a symptom was scored as an affirmative "Yes" response, with "No" and "Don't know" both scored as non-recognition. Associations between awareness and sociodemographic variables were tested using chi-square tests, independent-samples t-tests, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results The sample was 60.1% female, and the mean awareness score was 4.02 ± 2.02 out of 6. Shortness of breath (76.9%) and chest pain (75.8%) were recognized far more often than nausea or vomiting (50.9%) and jaw or neck pain (54.8%). At the participant level, 176/281 (62.6%) correctly recognized all three typical symptoms, 43/281 (15.3%) recognized two, 21/281 (7.5%) recognized one, and 41/281 (14.6%) recognized none. Nearly all participants (94.0%) knew that calling an ambulance was the appropriate first step, but only 26.7% incorrectly identified 997 as the national emergency number, while the majority (66.5%) correctly identified 911. Two-thirds of participants (66.9%) fell into the high-awareness group (≥ 4/6 symptoms recognized), but this did not differ significantly by gender (p = 0.506), education (p = 0.318), or age group (p = 0.914); mean awareness scores likewise showed no significant differences across these same groups (p = 0.379, 0.633, and 0.799, respectively). Conclusions Adults in Jeddah generally recognized classic MI symptoms and knew the correct emergency response, but recognition of atypical symptoms was lower and was not associated with the sociodemographic factors examined. Public health campaigns that specifically address atypical presentations, particularly nausea and jaw or neck pain, may be warranted for the population as a whole rather than targeting any single subgroup.

articles.title: Plasma mitochondrial-associated proteins scale with illness severity and predict outcome in suspected sepsis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in sepsis-related organ failure. We investigated whether plasma profiles of mitochondrial-associated proteins are associated with illness severity and short-term outcomes and explored whether they reveal distinct mitochondrial subphenotypes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this post hoc analysis of the Acutelines data-biobank, we included 213 adult patients presenting to the emergency department with a suspicion of sepsis, with infection confirmed by independent adjudication. Blood plasma proteins of patients were quantified with the Olink Explore HT platform; of 5,416 proteins, 232 mitochondrial-associated proteins (MitoCarta3.0) were z-standardized and averaged per patient to derive a continuous mitochondrial-protein score. To explore whether operationally distinct patient groups could be identified along this gradient, we additionally performed principal component analysis with K-means clustering on the same protein set. Differential abundance analysis, pathway enrichment, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression were performed as exploratory analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The continuous mitochondrial-associated protein score increased with illness severity (Spearman ρ 0.18-0.29; p < 0.01) and worse 72-hour outcomes (odds ratio per standard deviation: organ failure-free survival 0.57; intensive care unit admission 1.66; mortality 2.36). Exploratory clustering identified two groups differing mainly in overall mitochondrial-associated protein abundance. Considerable overlap and limited support for a discrete two-cluster structure suggested variation along a continuum rather than clearly distinct mitochondrial subphenotypes. Exploratory pathway analyses implicated mitochondrial metabolism, cellular stress, and injury-related processes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Higher plasma mitochondrial-associated protein abundance was associated with greater illness severity and worse short-term outcomes in suspected sepsis. These associations are hypothesis-generating, providing a first step toward understanding the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in sepsis severity.

articles.title: Screening Ultrasonography in a Basic Emergency Service for Suspected Acute Appendicitis: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Suspected acute appendicitis is a frequent clinical scenario in Basic Emergency Service (BES), particularly among patients presenting with acute abdominal pain. However, its clinical presentation is not always straightforward. In the early stages, symptoms may be nonspecific and overlap with other causes of abdominal pain, while the limited diagnostic resources available in peripheral emergency units may reduce the certainty of the initial clinical assessment. We present the case of a 22-year-old male who presented to a BES with acute abdominal pain associated with vomiting and food intolerance, with pain predominantly located in the lower abdominal quadrants and more evident on the right side. In the setting of a clinical presentation suggestive of acute appendicitis, screening ultrasonography was not intended to establish a definitive diagnosis but rather to add objective clinical information to the initial assessment and support a more reasoned decision regarding patient management. The identification of sonographic findings compatible with possible acute appendicitis strengthened the clinical suspicion and contributed to justifying central hospital referral. This case supports the potential role of screening ultrasonography as a complementary tool in peripheral or prehospital emergency settings, particularly when clinical findings are suggestive but insufficient to guide patient management with confidence. In such contexts, ultrasonography may help support decisions ranging from local treatment and discharge to hospital referral or follow-up by the patient's family physician.

articles.title: Suspected Pregabalin Overdose Presenting With Out-of-Hospital Asystolic Cardiac Arrest and Fatal Multiorgan Failure: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Pregabalin overdose is generally considered to have a relatively benign clinical course. However, severe respiratory depression, coma, and life-threatening clinical deterioration have rarely been reported, particularly in patients with high-dose ingestion or delayed recognition. We present the case of a 26-year-old male who was found unconscious following suspected intentional ingestion of approximately 14 pregabalin 300 mg capsules (4.2 g). On arrival of the emergency medical team, the patient was found to be in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of asystole. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 20 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. On admission, profound metabolic acidosis (pH: 6.43) and severe hyperlactatemia (lactate: 29 mmol/L) were present. During follow-up, the patient developed rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy, marked transaminase elevation compatible with ischemic hepatitis, and pancreatic enzyme elevation. Despite aggressive supportive treatment, the patient died on the fourth day due to refractory shock and multiorgan failure. Although pregabalin overdose is often benign, suspected high-dose ingestion may lead to profound central nervous system depression, loss of airway protective reflexes, aspiration, respiratory arrest, and fatal post-cardiac arrest multiorgan failure. Early airway protection and close hemodynamic monitoring are essential. We present a rare, fatal case of a young adult who developed multi-organ dysfunction syndrome following suspected severe pregabalin intoxication.

articles.title: Long-term survival of patients with persistent critical illness in Australia and New Zealand; a retrospective registry-based cohort study.
articles.journal_full: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To investigate whether increasing intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS) is associated with reduced long-term survival in patients with persistent critical illness (PerCI)(1,2) across Australian and New Zealand ICUs.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Population-based retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: All Australian and New Zealand ICUs reporting to the Australia and New Zealand Intensive Care Society's Adult Patient Database.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Adult patients (age >16) with an index admission to ICU from July 2019 to June 2024.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
abstract.text: All-cause mortality at 12, 24, and 60 months following ICU discharge in patients with PerCI. PerCI was defined as ICU length of stay (LOS) ≥10 d and was compared across five prespecified LOS categories: 10-13 d (reference group), 14-20, 21-29, 30-89, and ≥90 d.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 985,594 ICU admissions, 35,573 (3.6%) met the PerCI criterion. Survival from ICU discharge was ∼70% at 12 m and varied between 47.5% and 61.4% at 60 m across LOS groups. After adjustment for illness severity, age, frailty, and comorbidity, LOS was not independently associated with survival in the ICU length of stay (ICU LOS) 21-29- and 30-89-day groups when compared with the 10-13-day group; however, the 14-20-day group (hazard ratio [HR] 1.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]:1.02-1.11, p = 0.005) and ≥90-d group (HR 1.31, 95% CI: 1.06-1.61, p = 0.011) had higher hazard of death. The strongest predictors of shorter survival were chronic liver disease (HR 1.76, 95% CI: 1.62-1.92, p < 0.001), frailty (HR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.38-1.51, p < 0.001), and dialysis-dependent renal failure (HR 1.34, 95% CI: 1.23-1.45, p < 0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Most patients with PerCI in Australia and New Zealand had favourable long-term survival. After adjustment, the ≥90-day group emerged as a distinct exception, with a significantly higher hazard of death and five-year survival below 50%, despite its small size (N = 226). In contrast, ICU length of stay (ICU LOS) was not independently associated with survival across the 10-89-day range, indicating that for most patients, outcome is determined by underlying characteristics rather than time in the ICU. Future work should examine functional outcomes, frailty trajectory, quality of life, out of hospital resource use, and the characteristics distinguishing survivors from nonsurvivors.

articles.title: Biohacking Recovery: The Cutting Edge in Facial Plastic Surgery.
articles.journal: Facial Plast Surg Clin North Am
articles.journal_full: Facial plastic surgery clinics of North America

abstract.text: The traditional "rest and wait" approach to surgical recovery is being replaced by proactive biohacking strategies designed to optimize patient biology. This paper explores "pre-covery" and postoperative protocols that modulate systemic stress responses and facilitate repair. By integrating modalities such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy, and photobiomodulation, surgeons can actively accelerate tissue repair and improve aesthetic outcomes. Coupled with supplementation and emerging regenerative peptides, these strategies represent a paradigm shift toward a more thoughtfully planned perioperative recovery approach in facial plastic surgery.

articles.title: The Benefit of Early Advanced Airway Management Depends on Prehospital Epinephrine Timing in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The combined effect of epinephrine and advanced airway management (AAM) timing on out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) outcomes remains poorly characterized.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To investigate the interaction between epinephrine and AAM timing and their joint association with neurological and survival outcomes in OHCA.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective study used Korea OHCA Registry data (August 2019-December 2023). We included adults receiving prehospital epinephrine and AAM. Epinephrine timing was early (=10 min) or late (>10 min) from emergency medical services arrival; AAM timing was early (=6 min) or late (>6 min). This yielded four groups: early epinephrine/early AAM (EE-EA), early epinephrine/late AAM (EE-LA), late epinephrine/early AAM (LE-EA), and late epinephrine/late AAM (LE-LA). Multivariable logistic regression and interaction analyses were performed for good neurological recovery (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2), survival to discharge, and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 20,662 eligible patients, 37.1% were in the EE-EA group. Compared with LE-LA, the EE-EA group had significantly higher odds of good neurological recovery (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.93-3.08) and survival to discharge (aOR 2.18, 95% CI 1.87-2.55). The LE-EA group showed no significant benefit over LE-LA (aOR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71-1.40). A significant interaction between early epinephrine and early AAM was observed for neurological recovery (aOR 1.45, 95% CI 1.08-1.95; p=0.045).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Early epinephrine combined with early AAM was associated with optimal neurological recovery. However, this multiplicative interaction was attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing resuscitation time bias, suggesting a hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory association.

articles.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy for Cognitive Impairment Resulting from Neurological Disorders: Mechanisms of Action and Application Advances.

abstract.text: Cognitive impairment is a common and disabling consequence of various neurological disorders. Due to its high prevalence, high conversion rate, and significant burden, it has increasingly become a major challenge for aging societies worldwide. Existing treatment strategies have limited efficacy in halting disease progression, making effective intervention strategies urgently needed. As a non-invasive physical therapy, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) exerts its effects by increasing arterial oxygen partial pressure and improving tissue oxygenation. Historically widely used for treating carbon monoxide poisoning and decompression sickness, HBOT has recently demonstrated potential in alleviating symptoms of neurological disorders. Mechanistically, HBOT modulates the hypoxic microenvironment, promotes angiogenesis, restores neurovascular integrity, enhances neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity, and reduces neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. This paper systematically reviews the mechanisms of action, application progress, and existing limitations of HBOT in neurological disorders causing cognitive impairment. As a promising therapeutic modality, HBOT holds the potential to overcome current treatment limitations and become a key component of comprehensive neurological rehabilitation strategies.

articles.title: Assessment of Prehospital Emergency Personnel's Knowledge in Pediatric Anaphylaxis Management.
articles.journal_full: Iranian journal of allergy, asthma, and immunology

abstract.text: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapidly progressing, and potentially life-threatening emergency requiring prompt, evidence-based intervention. This study assessed pre-hospital emergency healthcare professionals' knowledge of anaphylaxis diagnosis, acute management, and treatment protocols in line with current clinical guidelines. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted between February and April 2025 among physicians, paramedics, and emergency medical technicians (EMTs) working in Emergency Medical Services (EMS) stations. Data were collected via a 21-item Google Forms survey covering demographics and key knowledge domains based on established pediatric anaphylaxis guidelines. A total of 322 professionals participated: paramedics (n = 214, 66.5%), EMTs (n = 73, 22.7%), and physicians (n = 35, 10.9%). Although most reported prior anaphylaxis training (90.0%) and clinical encounters (87.6%), only 52.2% correctly identified all three diagnostic criteria. Regarding pharmacologic management, 81.7% recognized epinephrine as first-line treatment, with physicians performing best (94.3%) compared to paramedics (81.8%) and EMTs (75.3%). Similarly, 81.1% correctly identified the intramuscular route, with physicians again demonstrating superior knowledge (95.5%). However, major deficiencies were noted in appropriate patient positioning (52.2%) and epinephrine auto-injector use (50.6%), with significant inter-professional differences across both domains. Substantial knowledge gaps exist among pre-hospital emergency providers regarding anaphylaxis diagnosis, patient positioning, and auto-injector administration. Targeted training and standardized protocols are urgently needed to enhance competency and improve patient safety in pre-hospital anaphylaxis management.

articles.title: Treatment of Diseases in the Civil Society of the Han Empire.

abstract.text: The separation of medicine and shamanism, which began during the Spring and Autumn Period, led to the emergence of "excellent physicians" who were distinct from shamans, a trend that continued from the Warring States Period through the early Han Dynasty. However, while there were some instances of these highly skilled physicians treating commoners, their medical practice was primarily concentrated among the ruling elite-including rulers, high-ranking officials, and those associated with them. Furthermore, physicians with outstanding treatment records in the general populace were sought after by the imperial court, the central government, feudal lords, and local administrative offices; many excellent physicians consequently flocked to the capital, Chang'an, or regional centers, where they were offered substantial compensation. Consequently, patients in the grassroots of society, who found it difficult to receive treatment from these skilled physicians, had no choice but to rely on shamans for their medical care. Folk healers served, on the one hand, as shamans and priests, and on the other, as practitioners who treated common ailments through methods such as acupuncture and herbal medicine. The state, too, dispatched physicians from the imperial court or local administrative offices to the general public to provide relief during special circumstances, such as the outbreak of infectious diseases. During the Han Dynasty, those who supplied medicinal herbs for the treatment of illnesses in civilian society included the "mu-ui" and recluses documented in historical records, as well as anonymous herb gatherers not mentioned in those records. They supplied civilian society with approximately 130 types of herbal medicines, including ginseng, as evidenced by the herbal records unearthed to date. A significant number of them possessed medical knowledge and helped treat the common people's illnesses. Furthermore, while it was relatively easy to obtain medicinal herbs in the capital, Chang'an, or in provincial centers, the farther one traveled from these areas, the more difficult it became to procure them, and their prices were often beyond the means of ordinary people. Furthermore, at that time, many people believed that illness was "a calamity brought on by spirits," and for them, treating an illness meant driving out spirits and evil entities. Consequently, incantations performed by shamans were widely practiced as a method of healing and, taking the form of sympathetic magic, even extended to natural objects. The common people of that era also actively engaged in magical healing through methods such as "chukyu."

articles.title: The Gradual Establishment and Historical Implications of Hospital Ship Mobile Medical Services along Korea's Western and Southern Coasts in the 1960s-1970s.

abstract.text: The term muui (doctorless) refers to a state of absolute deprivation of medical care. In modern Korean history, chronic shortages and regional disparities of medical resources resulted in the widespread existence of muuichon (doctorless village). In response, the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs implemented a series of policies and initiatives, including the establishment of a public health center system and the mobilization of public doctors. Yet the very term muuichon also suggested that the problem of public health was inseparable from that of space. Above all, there was a distinct spatial hierarchy of medical accessibility, extending from the capital, Seoul, to major cities, smaller cities, rural villages, and, finally, to remote mountainous and island regions. Among these areas, the islands along the western and southern coast faced significant geographical obstacles, making even minimal access to medical services exceedingly difficult. Hospital ships emerged as a historical product of this intertwined medical-spatial context. By the mid-1960s, as the public doctor mobilization program came to an end, local health authorities and private medical institutions in island regions devised a plan to construct specialized ships equipped with medical facilities and dispatch them to circulate among muuido (doctorless island). Consequently, Korea's first hospital ships, Gyeonggi and Badaui Byeol, began operations and helped fill the gap left by the absence of medical institutions in island regions. In doing so, they moved beyond conventional approaches tied to fixed administrative boundaries and pioneered a healthcare delivery system adaptable to the region's distinctive spatial characteristics. Moreover, this system demonstrated its effectiveness by requiring relatively modest expenditures while extending medical services to islands throughout the region. During the 1970s, the central government also came to recognize the advantages of this system and sought to institutionalize mobile medical services aboard hospital ships. In the mid-to-late 1970s, in particular, President Park Chung Hee spearheaded the construction of numerous hospital ships, thereby establishing the material foundation for the system. In 1978, the island regions along the western and southern coasts were reorganized into nine medical service districts, each assigned one or two hospital ships under the newly established Hospital Ship Medical Service District System. As a result, the system followed a reversed trajectory in which an initiative first pioneered at the local level was subsequently integrated into and institutionalized at the national level. This process exemplifies a dimension of dynamism in South Korean medical administration that cannot be fully captured through a state-centered perspective or adequately explained by structural accounts based solely on budgets or fiscal considerations. Yet, in the final phase of institutionalization, President Park Chung Hee intervened directly to bring the matter to a definitive conclusion, thereby also reinforcing the image of his rule as benevolent.

articles.title: Customizing and fine-tuning opioid overdose machine learning models for community-specific dashboards.

abstract.text: Drug overdose is a leading cause of death in the United States. Targeted community interventions and allocation of resources for reducing overdose deaths require timely and actionable data to make a meaningful public health impact. We present our work on tuning geographic-specific machine learning forecast models to predict the number of opioid-involved overdoses involving Emergency Medical Services (EMS) in Kentucky, with a focus on optimizing covariates representing measurable opioid overdose risk and protective factors. We aggregated suspected opioid-involved overdoses in EMS data into monthly totals by county between January 2017 and September 2025. We further grouped these counties into larger regions, representing Area Development Districts (ADDs), service areas for Community Mental Health Centers (CMHCs), and local health departments (LHDs). We constructed long-term time-series forecasting models (NLinear LTSF) to predict opioid-involved overdoses three months into the future. We tested the impact of using eight covariate data sources: Kentucky State Police drug seizures, Medicaid claims, community naloxone distribution, Kentucky Department of Corrections intakes and releases, social determinants of health data, location of treatment venues, and weather. We evaluated our models using both an unseen 10% test set and an expanding window strategy, where we simulated predicting historical data and retrained the model using data available for every three-month window. We embedded predictions into community-specific dashboards where end-users can select individual counties, or larger regions covered by distinct ADDs, CMHCs, or LHDs. The dashboards are integrated in Kentucky's Rapid Actionable Data for Opioid Response system designed to deliver ongoing near-real time analytics and forecasting at state and local levels.

articles.title: When No ICU Bed is Available: Critical Care Services in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: This review article, focused on the care of the critically ill adult when no intensive care unit (ICU) bed is available, describes current models addressing critical care services in the emergency department (ED), reviews available evidence on the impact of different approaches, and explores best practices in implementation of ED-ICU models. Based on these findings, the article explores potential benefits of leveraging the ED-ICU concept in the regional organization of critical care services.

articles.title: Facial Diplegia Guillain-Barre Syndrome Variant Initially Presenting as a Stroke Mimic: Evolution from Unilateral Central-Appearing Facial Weakness to Bilateral Facial Palsy - A Case Report.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Facial diplegia is an uncommon regional variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). It may initially resemble acute cerebrovascular disease when facial weakness appears unilateral or central in pattern.

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 48-year-old Sri Lankan man with untreated hypertension, obesity, and newly recognized diabetes presented approximately 18 h after onset of slurred speech and persistent left facial weakness. Initial examination suggested a left central facial palsy, although incomplete left eye closure was also present. Non-contrast computed tomography and same-day brain magnetic resonance imaging with angiography, performed approximately 25 h after symptom onset, showed no acute infarction, hemorrhage, vascular occlusion, dissection, or significant stenosis. Over the next 48 h, facial weakness progressed to bilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy with mild dysphagia and weak gag reflex, while limb strength remained preserved. Cerebrospinal fluid showed albuminocytologic dissociation. Dedicated contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the internal auditory canals showed no facial nerve enhancement; bilateral linear enhancement represented vascular enhancement. Electrodiagnostic testing showed facial motor terminal latency abnormalities, prolonged bilateral blink reflex responses, and facial muscle EMG abnormalities supportive of a facial diplegia GBS variant. Campylobacter testing and anti-ganglioside antibody testing were not performed. He received intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and gradually improved.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Facial diplegia GBS may initially trigger an acute stroke evaluation when early facial weakness appears unilateral or central. Repeated neurological examination, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and neurophysiology are essential when persistent symptoms and negative neuroimaging argue against a vascular syndrome.

articles.title: Simulation-based training to enhance emergency response in low-resource settings - a model for paramedic education in Ghana.
articles.journal_full: Annals of agricultural and environmental medicine : AAEM

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Despite targeted investments in acute care in Ghana, significant challenges persist, including limited medical supplies, shortages of trained personnel, and restricted access to medications. A key barrier to effective prehospital care is the lack of formal education among paramedics. To address this gap, the Paramedics for Africa 3 programme was implemented between July - December 2020, aimed at improving emergency medical knowledge and skills among healthcare providers.

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: A pre-post intervention design was used to evaluate the impact of the training. A total of 268 participants, including paramedics, hospital staff, and outpatient clinic workers, were enrolled. Each completed a 50-question multiple-choice test covering anatomy, diagnostics, and medical procedures. The programme included hands-on activities, simulation-based scenarios, and case-based learning. Statistical analysis was used to assess changes in test performance.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Baseline test scores ranged from 14% - 76% (median: 40%), increasing post-training to 32% -100% (median: 76%; p < 0.001). The most notable improvements were observed in trauma care and resuscitation. Emergency service staff demonstrated the most significant gains (p = 0.03). No statistically significant differences were found in terms of age, gender, education, or residence.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The programme led to a significant improvement in participants' knowledge of emergency medicine. The positive impact of simulation-based learning highlights the importance of expanding such educational models in resource-limited healthcare settings.

articles.title: Strategies to Manage Refractory Hypoxemia in the Intubated Patient.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Persistent hypoxemia after intubation is associated with high mortality and demands a systematic approach focused on the underlying pathophysiology. This article emphasizes developing a focused differential diagnosis that includes both mechanical and patient factors to guide management. The authors review key therapeutic strategies, including careful use of positive end expiratory pressure, positioning techniques, medications such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, sedation, and neuromuscular blockade, and, when conventional therapies fail, consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.

articles.title: Emergency Burn Resuscitation: Where Evidence Meets Practice.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: The initial management of a critically ill burn patient sets the trajectory for their entire hospital course. Understanding standards of care is essential, but moving beyond rote formulas for airway management, fluids, and analgesia is critical to ensuring appropriate care and preventing iatrogenic harm. This article provides an evidence-based guide for emergency physicians on when and how to pivot from standard care to nuanced, life-saving interventions that address the dynamic pathophysiology of severe burns.

articles.title: Refractory Shock in the Post-Cardiac Arrest Patient.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Mixed shock is common after cardiac arrest (CA), with dominant shock physiology sometimes changing over the course of hours. This article focuses on identifying dominant shock physiology in patients with refractory shock after CA and targeted strategies for resuscitation. The authors discuss approach to cardiogenic shock, including pharmacologic and mechanical support, as well as advanced pharmacologic therapies relevant to distributive shock.

articles.title: Management of the Critically Ill Patient with Opioid Use Disorder.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: The management of critically ill patients with opioid use disorder presents a unique challenge, as overdose, withdrawal, or concomitant intoxication, due to an unregulated drug supply, leads to physiologic changes that potentially impact standard treatment. This review article outlines an emergency medicine-focused approach for early recognition and stabilization of opioid overdose or withdrawal. Topics include naloxone, use of medications for opioid use disorder, recognition of concurrent intoxication, treatment of α2-agonist withdrawal, multimodal analgesia, and sedation for opioid-tolerant patients. The acute management of opioid use disorder is an opportunity to prevent withdrawal-related decompensation, improve comfort, and support ongoing engagement in treatment.

articles.title: Managing the Critically Ill Postpartum Patient in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: This review article prepares emergency physicians to recognize and manage critical illness in postpartum patients, a population at heightened risk of preventable morbidity and mortality in North America amid persistent racial/geographic disparities and shrinking obstetric access. It highlights key physiologic changes after delivery that complicate patient management. The article focuses on 3 immediate postpartum emergencies (postpartum hemorrhage, postpartum preeclampsia, and amniotic fluid embolism) and 3 subacute (pulmonary embolism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection). It concludes with system-level strategies to improve safety and outcomes.

articles.title: Securing the Airway, Protecting the Brain: Neuroprotective Intubation for Acute Neurologic Emergencies.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Emergency airway management in acute brain injury carries unique physiologic risks, such as hypotension, hypoxia, hypercarbia, and sympathetic surges can precipitate secondary brain injury. This review outlines a neuroprotective approach focused on deliberate preparation, physiologic optimization, and evidence-informed techniques. Key elements include rapid ABCD assessment, recognition of elevated intracranial pressure, appropriate use of hyperosmolar therapy, strategies to blunt sympathetic surges, tailored induction and paralysis, techniques to maximize first-pass success, and postintubation ventilation and sedation aimed at maintaining eucapnia, normoxia, and stable cerebral perfusion. This approach reframes intubation as an opportunity to prevent secondary injury and improve outcomes.

articles.title: The Architecture of Preparation: How Effective Emergency Medicine Teams Prepare for Complexity and Uncertainty.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: This article reframes preparation for critically ill patients as a dynamic, compounding process that spans 3 temporal phases: strategic, operational, and reflective. Using concepts such as shared mental models, psychological safety, adaptive capacity, and the 3A's prebriefing framework (anticipate, align, and adapt), the article outlines how teams can better navigate uncertainty and complexity in real time. This article describes the consequences of preparation deficit and preparation debt, and provide practical tactics for rapid appraisal, decision-making in motion, and structured reflection. Together, these strategies create a preparation architecture that enhances performance, reduces error, and strengthens team and system resilience.

articles.title: The Non-invasive Hemodynamic Profile: A Modern Approach to the Evaluation and Management of Acute Decompensated Heart Failure-Related Cardiogenic Shock with Point-of-Care Ultrasound.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Emergency department presentations of acute decompensated heart failure-related cardiogenic shock (ADHF-CS) are increasing and are associated with high short-term mortality. Early diagnosis is challenging due to variable clinical presentation, compensatory physiology, and limited availability of invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Point-of-care ultrasound enables quick, noninvasive assessment of cardiac output, right atrial pressure, and systemic vascular resistance. This review outlines a practical bedside echocardiographic approach to generate a rapid hemodynamic profile in suspected ADHF-CS, facilitating accurate phenotyping and targeted resuscitation strategies in the emergency setting.

articles.title: Safely Transferring the Critically Ill Patient out of Your Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Regionalized systems of care increasingly rely on critical care transport (CCT) to move high-acuity patients to centers with specialized resources. This article outlines the complex clinical, operational, and ethical considerations that shape interfacility transport, emphasizing the need for deliberate risk-benefit assessment, patient optimization, and clear communication among sending clinicians, transport teams, and receiving facilities. Variability in CCT team training, capabilities, and staffing models requires clinicians to understand regional resources. By applying systems-based thinking and the "right patient, right time, right team, right place" framework, clinicians can ensure safe, equitable, high-quality transport within regionalized care networks.

articles.title: Troubleshooting the Failed Airway.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: The failed airway is a high-stakes event arising from deranged physiology, challenging anatomy, and technical difficulty. Mitigation requires proactive resuscitation of the physiologically difficult airway and optimizing oral intubation techniques. Key procedural strategies include airway checklist use during all airways, prioritizing video laryngoscopy, employing progressive suction methods like suction-assisted laryngoscopy for airway decontamination, and using a bougie-first approach for introducer selection. When oral intubation fails, providers must be proficient in advanced techniques such as flexible bronchoscopy and emergency front-of-neck access. Simulation and continuous quality assurance are essential to maintain competency in troubleshooting the failed airway.

articles.title: Posterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Elite Athletes: A Narrative Review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries are uncommon in sport but may be career-defining for elite athletes. Controversy remains regarding indications for reconstruction, optimal techniques and the role of braced non-operative care. This narrative review summarises evidence on operative and non-operative management of PCL injuries in elite athletes, focusing on return-to-play (RTP), graft selection, reconstruction strategy and elite-specific considerations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A narrative review was conducted in PubMed and Embase (inception-April 2025) with reference list screening. Clinical studies reporting return-to-play outcomes after operative or non-operative management of isolated PCL injuries and PCL-based MLKIs in athletic cohorts were prioritised; 51 studies were included, and heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Isolated PCL injuries in elite footballers are rare, whereas PCL-based multi-ligament knee injuries (MLKIs) are more common in collision sports. Early dynamic bracing with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation enables > 90% RTP in selected acute isolated grade II-III tears in high-level athletic cohorts (Level III evidence). For chronic instability or MLKIs, anatomic single-bundle reconstruction remains common, with double-bundle and tibial inlay approaches offering biomechanical but limited clinical advantages. Modern elite MLKI cohorts report 80-90% RTP, though full return-to-performance is less frequent.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Management of elite PCL injuries requires individualised, sport-specific decision-making that balances biological healing with performance demands. High-quality, sport-specific outcome data remain limited.Level of EvidenceLevel V, narrative review.

articles.title: Modern Approach to Vascular Access in the Critically Ill Patient.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Vascular access is a key intervention in the management of critically ill emergency department patients. This can include peripheral or central venous access and intraosseous access. In combination with arterial catheterization, central venous access can provide key information to guide volume and vasoactive medication titration in isolation as well as in combination with dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness. This article will review the indications and contraindications as well as decision-making for the use of these modalities in light of the current evidence.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Decision Support in Orthopaedic Emergencies: A Review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Orthopaedic emergencies require rapid, accurate clinical decisions to prevent limb- and life-threatening complications. Increasing patient volume, limited specialist availability, and diagnostic complexity contributes to delays and errors in emergency care. Artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) and has emerged as a promising tool to augment decision-making in orthopaedic emergencies.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To review current applications, evidence, limitations, and future directions of AI-based decision-support systems in orthopaedic emergency care, with particular relevance to low- and middle-income healthcare settings.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A comprehensive electronic search was performed in major academic databases. This included PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify all relevant literature published in English from inception up to February 2026, focusing on AI applications in orthopaedic trauma, emergency imaging, triage, clinical decision support, and outcome prediction. Emphasis was placed on clinically validated studies, systematic reviews, and emerging technologies relevant to emergency orthopaedics.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: AI applications in orthopaedic emergencies primarily included automated fracture detection, injury classification, triage optimisation, clinical decision support, and complication prediction. DL models have demonstrated diagnostic accuracy comparable to or exceeding that of expert clinicians in fracture detection. AI-assisted triage systems reportedly outperformed conventional scoring tools in predicting severity and admission needed based on the studies included for this review. Clinical decision-support tools improved the completeness and consistency of emergency management recommendations based on hospital-based and practice-oriented studies. The reported challenges included those related to data bias, interpretability, clinical integration, ethical concerns, and regulatory oversight.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: AI has substantial potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and decision-making in orthopaedic emergencies. Responsible adoption requires robust external validation, clinician education, explainable models, and integration into existing workflows. When appropriately implemented, AI can serve as a valuable adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, clinical expertise in orthopaedic emergency care.

articles.title: Post-intubation Sedation and Analgesia in the Emergency Department: The Basics and Beyond.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Provision of postintubation sedation and analgesia is critical in emergency management of mechanically ventilated patients. Pain and sedation should be monitored using a validated scoring system, and medications titrated to a target sedation level, which should usually be light. Usually, fentanyl is the first-line analgesic and propofol is the first-line sedative. Dexmedetomidine and ketamine may be helpful in select populations, but further research is needed to define their role in the emergency department. Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided. Physicians should plan for postintubation sedation and analgesia in advance and consider using succinylcholine for intubation to avoid awareness with paralysis.

articles.title: Titrating and Discontinuing Noninvasive Respiratory Support in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

abstract.text: Acute respiratory failure is common in the emergency department (ED), often requiring noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS). NIRS has become a cornerstone in the initial management of acute respiratory failure. Despite its growing use, significant variability in practice remains, and evidence-based guidance specific to the ED setting is limited. This article aims to provide emergency physicians with a practical, evidence-informed framework for initiating and managing NIRS in adults with acute respiratory failure, with a focus on initial settings, titration, monitoring for failure, and guidance on weaning and liberation.

articles.title: REPRINTED FROM THE 2023 HYPERBARIC INDICATIONS MANUAL 15TH EDITION:Randomized Controlled Trials in Hyperbaric Medicine.
articles.journal_full: Undersea & hyperbaric medicine : journal of the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society, Inc

abstract.text: The criticism has been made of hyperbaric medicine that treatment is based on little or no good clinical evidence. Recently, improved awareness among medical practitioners of the importance of evidence has highlighted this perception, as has the proliferation of both funder-generated reviews and technology assessments [1-3]. In fact, many clinical randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating the application of hyperbaric oxygen (HBO₂) therapy have been reported, albeit of variable quality. It is the purpose of this review to describe the place of RCTs within the practice of evidence-based medicine (EBM), summarize the methods by which such trials can be located, discuss the appraisal and performance of RCTs with specific reference to hyperbaric medicine, and to provide a list of RCTs and meta-analyses in hyperbaric medicine to date. Particular reference is made to the work of the Cochrane Collaboration within the field. An appendix provides a comprehensive list of published RCTs and meta-analyses arranged by indication (Appendix 1). To date, this list includes 416 citations of 390 trials.

articles.title: UHMS Position Statement: Standardization of Terminology in Undersea and Hyperbaric Medicine: Adoption of "Hyperbaric Oxygen Treatment".
articles.journal_full: Undersea & hyperbaric medicine : journal of the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society, Inc

abstract.text: Hyperbaric medicine terminology has historically lacked standardization, with multiple terms and abbreviations used interchangeably across clinical practice, scientific publications, educational materials, and public communications. Inconsistent nomenclature may contribute to confusion regarding the definition, regulation, clinical standards, and physician oversight associated with hyperbaric oxygen treatment. The Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society (UHMS) endorses the term hyperbaric oxygen treatment as the preferred terminology for clinically delivered hyperbaric oxygen under accepted UHMS standards. The Society recommends adoption of the abbreviation HBO₂ or HBO₂ treatment in place of HBOT across manuscripts, presentations, educational content, and operational documents. Consistent nomenclature is intended to improve clarity and communication among clinicians, researchers, regulatory agencies, payers, referring providers, and the public.

articles.title: Bubbles or microparticles: which are the main initial cause of decompression illness?
articles.journal_full: Undersea & hyperbaric medicine : journal of the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society, Inc

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: There are two leading schools of thought on the mechanism that causes decompression illness (DCI). The old school attributes DCI to decompression bubbles, while the new school, mostly led by S. Thom, attributes DCI mainly to microparticles (MP).

abstract.label: MICROPARTICLES
abstract.text: Microparticles were found to be elevated at high pressures before decompression and, more so, after decompression. Decompression MP activate neutrophils and platelets, enhance inflammation, stimulate proinflammatory cytokines, and proto-coagulant activity. The predominant presence of endothelial MP is obvious. It was suggested that large MP contain a gas phase of nitric oxide (NO) and its derivatives and serve as gas micronuclei for decompression bubbles. Formation of a gas phase from very soluble NO is unlikely.

abstract.label: BUBBLES
abstract.text: Bubbling is crucial in the decompression from depth, and one cannot simply shoot up from the depth to the surface. The inconsistency between the relations of venous bubbles and DCI can be related to DCI unrelated to shunted/non-shunted venous bubbles, like distal arterial bubbles and local bubble formation. It was suggested that a detached bubble tears off the underlying endothelial cells, and when the bubble becomes lodged in the lung, it diminishes to a gas-containing microparticle enveloped by an endothelial membrane.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The main initial cause for DCI is the formation of decompression bubbles, and microparticles add to the injury but would not cause DCI without decompression bubbles.

articles.title: A Critical Look at Soft-Sided and Hard-Sided "Mild" Hyperbaric Chambers - Risks, Regulations, and Ethical Oversights.
articles.journal_full: Undersea & hyperbaric medicine : journal of the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society, Inc

abstract.text: Soft-sided hyperbaric chambers, as well as some hard-sided (mild) hyperbaric chambers, which are low-pressure, hyperbaric chambers that are typically designed for operational pressures of 3-5psi, have gained popularity in recent years. They are marketed as safe and effective for various conditions but lack compliance with critical regulatory and safety standards and codes. This raises concerns regarding patient safety, the validity of manufacturers' claims, and the ethical obligations of medical professionals and regulators. This manuscript examines the risks, regulatory gaps, and ethical implications of using soft-sided fabric chambers, as well as hard-sided (mild) hyperbaric chambers, focusing on their failure to meet FDA clearance, NFPA 99 & NFPA 101 codes, and ASME-PVHO standards. A comprehensive review of regulatory guidelines, safety reports, and marketing practices was conducted, supplemented by illustrations of adverse events linked to the use of these devices. Ethical principles, including beneficence, non-maleficence, and informed consent, were applied to analyze the responsibilities of manufacturers, healthcare providers, patients, and regulators. These chambers are often marketed with misleading claims about their efficacy and safety. Their non-compliance with FDA clearance, as well as not following industry standards and safety codes increases the risk of patient harm, including otic and pulmonary barotrauma, suffocation, fire hazards, structural failure, and, in extreme cases, death. Regulatory oversight remains inconsistent, allowing manufacturers to exploit loopholes. Furthermore, ethical concerns arise when patients are not fully informed of the limitations and risks of these devices. The widespread use of these hyperbaric chambers poses significant safety and ethical challenges. Stricter enforcement of regulatory standards and codes, transparent marketing practices, and ethical accountability from healthcare providers and manufacturers are essential to protect patients and uphold public trust in medical technologies.

articles.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in Septic Shock: A First-in-Human Pilot Trial.
